speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Minister of Transport. speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. It is not a matter of a large number of rail line abandonment applications awaiting hearing before the board. It is rather a case of large numbers of notices of intention to apply having been filed with the board. This was done at the request of the government so there would be available, when policies were being worked out, some idea of what was involved, and in this way there would be an appreciation of the possible problems facing the policy makers. It is quite improper to refer to these as applications for abandonment, because great numbers of them may never become applications for abandonment and may never be proceeded with. But getting the notices of intention forward so we would have some idea of what could be involved in the problem is very important.
Coming to the other part of the question, Mr. Speaker, it is, as I think I indicated earlier, the intention of the government to proceed with legislation on many parts of the

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wonder whether I may just say a word about this item, which will then be explained by my colleague the Minister of Labour. It will be noted, sir, that this is an item to supplement the miscellaneous minor or unforeseen vote of the Department of Finance which appears in the main estimates. While it is quite unusual for a supplementary to be voted before the main item is voted, this is partly the result of the calendar and the fact that we had an election and the estimates are not coming along at the ordinary time.
The purpose of this vote is to provide funds to carry out one of the programs announced by my hon. friend the Minister of Labour on June 10 last. It was thought that in order to be quite sure there would not be any financial problem about going ahead with any of this work, it should be brought before the house at this stage. That is the reason for doing it. The reason for putting it in this particular vote is that it is contemplated that the actual expenditures will be made, as is the case with this vote ordinarily, in various other departments and transferred from this finance vote to the other departments in the normal way of which hon. members who have sat on treasury board are well aware.
We were advised by the officials of the treasury board that under our procedures this was the most satisfactory way of dealing with this problem. I had some doubt, I must confess on reflection, after making the announcement last night that I would ask for the vote, about whether I had been properly in order since the Department of Finance have not been called after the supply motion. I spoke to the hon. gentlemen opposite and also consulted the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who I readily admit knows a lot more about the rules than I do-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Only when he agrees with the minister.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is not always right either-and he persuaded me that it is probably in order, almost certainly in order in a technical sense, to proceed with this vote. I am prepared to say that if any hon. member, because of the unusual character of the procedure, felt that it was not a proper thing to do at this time the government would not proceed with it.

Mr. Chairman, it is so unusual to hear the hon. gentleman speak with uncertainty of his opinion that I am sure the house would, under the circumstances, be willing to do anything to approve a request on his part. He usually lectures the house as to what it should or should not do, and speaks with an extra authority. Today he spoke with that diffidence and concern with

Supply^Finance
which all good house leaders speak when they have to bring about something that is not altogether proper. That he should have made an error in his interpretation of the rules has always been excusable, because after all Homer himself once nodded. Having said that, I think we on this side of the house, in view of the explanation, would be entirely prepared to go on with this procedure.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I want to thank the right hon. gentleman without any reservation for his kind, and I think salutary, observations.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, might I have the privilege of saying a word or two along this line. I think of occasions in the past when as house leader I suggested even minor alterations in the business which was before the house, and I was from time to time subjected to considerable invective and sharp attacks from the present Secretary of State and his colleague who is now Minister of Justice. I also carried the burden, in certain reports which appeared publicly, of delaying the business of the house and indulging in wrangling. I hope the present house leader will now realize some of the difficulties which confront the government house leader and that next year, when he will be house leader of the Liberal opposition, he will realize that co-operation with the government house leader is sometimes the best way of expediting the business of parliament.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I will endeavour at all times, as long as I am on this side of the house, to show the same humility the hon. gentleman showed when he was here.

Mr. Chairman, if there is any problem as to the propriety of taking this action today we in this group would give unanimous consent, although we do not think there is any difficulty in that respect. I should like to comment for a moment on the remark made by the Secretary of State to the effect that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre knew a whole lot more about the rules than he did. He also added that he is sometimes wrong. The only deduction I can make is that when the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is wrong he knows it.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: So do I.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I guess I had better stay out of this, although I would say to the present house leader and the former house leader, who have been having a very friendly exchange, that if at any time they are in difficulty and need someone to mediate between them I will be quite glad to [DOT]offer my services. We too are quite prepared, 4f- it is necessary, to give unanimous consent

to this procedure, but I am positive that this is not necessary. Rule 56 (6), which need not even be read, says quite clearly that a supplementary estimate is in the same category as interim supply, and I suggest that it is quite in order to go ahead.

Mr. Chairman, I should just like to ask the Secretary of State something for clarification purposes. Order No. 18 on the order paper refers to:
-main estimates and supplementary estimates (A) and (B) referred.
If I heard the chairman correctly he called only supplementary estimates (B) and we have them before us. 1 should like the Secretary of State to identify for us supplementary estimates (A) and tell us whether they are under consideration, or what they refer to.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Supplementary estimates (A) were the supplementary estimates which were tabled before we last asked for interim supply, and they covered all or most of the departments of government. The estimates for my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce have already been voted from (A). I take it that when, which I hope will not be long from now, we reach the estimates of my hon. friend the Minister of Transport, supplementary estimates (A) as well as the main estimates will both be before the committee when the items are called. We just wanted to dispose of this one first, and it was called separately. I think that is the correct explanation, and the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre seems to be indicating concurrence. I hope now, sir, that my hon. friend the Minister of Labour can tell us what the vote is about.

Mr. Chairman, my remarks on this item will be very brief. The house will recall that in June the government indicated that it intended to bring forward additional projects that had not been provided for in the main estimates. The purpose of this program was to help to alleviate particularly the problem of high seasonal winter unemployment.
The main estimates provided among other matters for both building and construction programs. I have been authorized by the government to ask various departments to bring forward additional projects for which moneys are not provided in the main estimates. The purpose of this item is to provide the moneys that will allow these projects to go forward. I should simply like to add that I have asked the various departments of government to bring forward projects which are justified on other grounds and which are in a state of readiness but which have not been provided for in the main estimates.

The item provides that these programs are subject to approval by treasury board, but I should like to add that they will also come forward to the Department of Labour for examination. The Department of Labour will attempt to assess the acceptance of these programs on two counts; first, that there should be sufficient labour content or employment content in these programs to justify their acceptance as an employment measure; and second, that these projects be undertaken in areas of high unemployment. It will not be the intention to bring forward additional projects under this item in areas in the country where there is not a specially high rate of unemployment. In other words this is an effort to deal with unemployment by providing additional programs with a justifiable labour content and to apply them in areas of high unemployment.

I should like to add just a few words to this discussion in view of what the Minister of Labour has said in trying to explain to the committee what this $7 million is intended to provide. All I have been able to gather is that this sum is being provided for the purpose of alleviating high seasonal unemployment and that certain departments are to undertake projects in order to help in this worth-while cause.
However, I feel we are being asked to approve an item which is somewhat hypothetical, at least with respect to the actual construction which is to be carried out by the various departments. Ordinarily public works required by each department are provided for in the main estimates, although occasionally supplementary estimates are introduced. It is usual for these projects to be carried out, at the request of the Department of Labour, at the time when seasonal unemployment is at its peak in order to help tide over that period. However, it seems that this is an additional amount, and the question which arises in my mind is this. Have the departments already planned certain projects, and what are those projects? What departments will be taking part in the expenditure of this $7 million?
It also seems odd to me that approval is apparently being sought for the expenditure of this $7 million without prior approval having been given by treasury board. The course usually followed, I believe, is that the department puts forward an estimate of expenditures. The estimate is approved by the treasury board, and only then is it brought before parliament for final approval. Here the minister is saying that parliament should approve first of all and that the item would then go- before treasury board for approval. I wonder if the minister could tell us what specific projects will be undertaken, which departments are likely to be participating, and
Supply-Finance
what plans they have with respect to the expenditure of this $7 million. I should also like the minister to give us some idea of the number of man hours of work the expenditure of this money is likely to provide.

Like my hon. friend the member for Ontario I am somewhat puzzled by the procedure which is being followed. We are being asked to vote $7 million under an item which was really not designed for the purpose to which the minister has referred. We know the purpose of the schedule of items in the estimates, and this is not the one normally used to help deal with employment problems. In effect we are being asked to write a blank cheque to the extent of $7 million, and obviously we should like to know which departments are likely to take advantage of this provision. After all, an estimate of $7 million has been made, so unless someone has picked the figure out of a hat and said "We shall hold them down to this" it should be possible to give the committee some idea of how the money is intended to be spent as among the various branches of government. In the light of the new love for planning which seems to have developed in certain quarters I would hardly think this is the way in which the government would have proceeded. Is most of this money likely to be spent by the Department of Transport, or by the Department of Public Works, or by-
Northern affairs.

Well, the department of northern affairs in the wintertime? That may be, but normally it would not be. I think the minister should give us some further information, because it seems to me we are being asked to write what is in effect a blank cheque for a grab bag fund.

I am interested in the formula which the department proposes to use in defining an area of high unemployment. What is the size of such an area likely to be? Would it be a constituency, or would it be larger? Finally, would the national employment service give the hon. gentleman advice on this matter or would it be some other branch or department?

I listened with interest to the minister's brief statement, and I want to take this opportunity to ask him a question or two because there seems to be some interesting happenings under the winter works program. When the hon. gentleman comes to reply, will he inform the committee as to the types of community organization other than incorporated municipalities which -are entitled - to qualify for grants under this program? I am thinking of privately owned

Supply-Finance
organizations. My second question is this. Is there any co-ordination between the Department of Labour and other departments of government when consideration is being given to the making of these grants?
I want to bring these circumstances to the attention of the minister. A certain fruit growing area in my constituency which has a considerable irrigation system was informed by the water controller of the province of British Columbia that it would be unwise for the growers to undertake any extensive or unusual repairs to the system because it was likely they would be flooded out in a year or two. Consequently no repairs were made. Then a hint was given that it might be possible to rebuild this irrigation system under the winter works program. An application was made accordingly, and I do not blame these people one bit for doing so. They proceeded to rebuild the irrigation system as a result of the assistance they received from the federal and provincial governments even though they had been previously informed by another department that it would not be required in another two or three years.
So we have the Secretary of State for External Affairs doing his best to see that these people are flooded under 25 feet of water, and at the same time we have the Department of Labour making grants to them against the advice of water board officials to assist them to rebuild a system which, it has been said, may not be needed. I would ask the minister to explain what degree of liaison there is among the various departments of government, who now appear to be working at cross purposes, and to tell us what types of organizations other than municipalities are entitled to receive grants under the winter works program.

Mr. Chairman, I am
going to begin by saying that the Minister of Labour is one minister who always tries to answer questions directed to him, and I have found that to be his regular course. It is in that spirit that I now ask him to inform the house how this $7 million is to be expended. What is the general plan? There must be something in mind. Surely it is not to be a case of expenditure without a policy. How is the amount going to be divided? Is it to be a melon that is to be cut in various segments depending upon the demand in the particular departments?
I am sure we could reduce the amount of debate very greatly if the minister would tell us what the circumstances are that have impelled this unusual course. What is the extra amount going to be used for? What department is it expected will be making the expenditure? I put this in capsule form
[Mr. Herridge.l
and ask him if he will not give hon. members this information now rather than wait, for after all the house has a right to know why such an unusual procedure of asking for $7 million over and above the regular amount of $3 million provided in the estimates is being followed. Would he be willing to advise the house now?
As the hon. member for Edmonton West has said, is this a blank cheque? My memory takes me back a few years to 1930. I recall the tremendous fulminations in the session in the fall of that year by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King when he spoke with authority and knowledge of the practice from the days of Runnymede to 1930, the need of parliament to have the fullest information, and said that nothing was more detrimental to responsible government than blank cheque advances made by parliament. I would ask the minister to give the house the fullest information he has. I am sure he must have it. The government is not asking for $7 million for the fun of it. It must know what it is going to do with it. The Minister of Finance has shown a propensity this session for asking for things about which there was no clarity in advance. I am sure the Minister of Labour does not want to join in the same company.

Mr. Chairman, when the
minister was speaking he expressed his desire that this money be spent on works with a very high labour content. I should like to remind the minister and his colleagues that the shipbuilding industry has the highest degree of labour content, and that if he refers to the Department of Transport and the Canadian maritime commission he will find a large shelf of plans for ships that could be quickly built. I know that $7 million will not build many ships, but having regard to the conditions in the country I am sure we will be faced with further supplementary estimates. Furthermore, now that the minister has been in charge of the department for some time and perhaps knows something about employment conditions in the country, I think it might be wise if he were to again look at the length of time that the winter works program will be applicable. If he could give the municipalities some assurance that the program would be extended they could then do a lot of planning for winter works now.

Mr. Chairman, I am quite agreeable to joining in the various suggestions that have been made that we get from the minister as much information as possible as to the purposes of the vote. I also support the suggestion made by the hon. member for

Kootenay West that there should be careful scrutiny and examination of the manner in which this money is spent.
However, in view of what I regard as the very modest sum being proposed in relation to the purposes outlined in an earlier statement to the house by the Minister of Labour, I was a little puzzled by the suggestion of the hon. member for Edmonton West that the whole question of planning was involved in the expenditure of this sum. If we were being asked to appropriate $700 million, then I should think that would be a very legitimate approach to take to the question. Somebody used the word "peanuts" the other day in the house, and in relation to the scope of the problem that needs to be dealt with it is my view that this item is really very modest.
If the minister were to request me to offer suggestions, I am quite sure I could put forward proposals with regard to my own constituency that would eat up most, if not all, of the $7 million. I am sure the minister is aware of the fact that we have a somewhat milder climate on Vancouver island than do some other parts of Canada, and that this would be a very pleasant place for some of those who in the past have normally been unemployed in the winter to find useful occupations. I think most hon. members are familiar with the fact that the level of unemployment in British Columbia in the wintertime tends to rise for the very reason that many Canadians are inclined to migrate or drift to that part of the country during the winter season.
As far as I am concerned, my reaction to this vote is that it is altogether too modest for the purposes which, according to the statements made by the Minister of Labour and the Secretary of State, the government has in mind. The Minister of Labour said something about accepting suggestions from the various departments of the government. I am not sure that he will be willing to accept suggestions from all members of the house in connection with the spending of this money, but I do know that in my own constituency, for example, there are a number of very useful public works projects, some of them with a substantial labour content, that have been postponed for one reason or another. Some of them went by the board because of what was referred to in the last parliament as the austerity program but which to me represented unnecessary delay in the provision of needed community projects and public services. I should like to suggest that the Minister of Labour should have raised his sights a little higher when he was
Supply-Finance
suggesting to his colleagues that this item should be brought forward in this way at this time.

Mr. Chairman, I will try to answer as well as I can the questions that have been raised by my hon. friends in connection with this item. I am sure that all of us are concerned about the prospect of seasonally high winter unemployment that has been characteristic of the Canadian economy. With that in mind I hope I can make the purpose of this item clear to hon. gentlemen.
There is now provision in the main estimates as we now have them for various projects. The officials of the Department of Labour and myself were of the view that it might be possible to bring forward additional projects for which funds were not provided in the main estimates. We had in mind that in the various departments there might be projects that were in a state of readiness and that could be brought forward quickly as a means of helping to relieve unemployment if additional funds were provided. There will be some departments that are especially affected, for example public works, transport, northern affairs, forestry and others.
I will ask all departments to bring forward projects that have not been provided for in the main estimates and which are in a state of readiness and capable of being put into effect during this winter period. I hope these projects will come forward and, as the hon. member for Ontario said, they will go before treasury board for justification just as other projects go before treasury board. At the same time there will be the additional provision that these projects will have to be justified, in so far as the labour department is concerned, from two points of view. First of all they must have sufficient labour content to justify them as job creating projects. I can imagine a project that could be brought forward that could be justified on other grounds but would not create any substantial amount of employment, or create relatively little employment. That is what will be done.
Then, where will these projects go? I want to assure the house that they will not be placed in various parts of the country on the basis of arbitrariness or caprice. The Department of Labour has developed over the years a concept of surplus manpower areas, related to the extent and duration of unemployment in those areas. When the former government brought in its double depreciation program this definition was changed and enlarged to designate areas that would be eligible for the double depreciation allowances.
Now, as you know, the present government, in line with this concept, has mentioned on

Supply-Finance
several occasions that it is proposing programs for special application to designated areas. Currently this concept of areas of high unemployment as defined by the Department of Labour is under review. There will be, when that review is completed and approved by the cabinet, particular areas in the country that are to be eligible for these special programs. It is to these areas that this special program will be applied.
And not outside?

Not outside of those areas; it is not intended to use this money except to assist unemployment in a manner that will be defined by the government through its designation of these areas in elaboration of the concept that was followed by the former government.
It is my hope that the department will be able to bring forward a sufficient number of projects that all this item will be used up. However, I cannot give that assurance today because I do not know what projects will ultimately come forward and be approved. It would be my hope that a large number of projects would qualify so that this total amount would be used up. Certainly, in so far as I am concerned, if it proved successful I would not mind asking my colleagues to provide an additional amount.
In essence that is the extent of the program or the purpose of the program. I agree that there is a certain element of the unknown in this because I cannot assure the committee what particular projects will qualify or whether the total sum will be completely used up, or indeed whether it is sufficient. I have attempted to indicate the general policy that will apply under this particular item.

Will the minister allow a question? Has there been any projection made by the Department of Labour as to the expected unemployment next winter? Has that been done as yet, and if so what is the number?

Mr. Chairman, I should like to tell my hon. friend that I have not recently received from the officials of the department any indication as to the extent of winter unemployment. I must say that shortly after I entered this office I had a discussion with my officials and the intimation at that time was-this is subject to my own memory-that the problem of unemployment might be greater this fall or next winter than it had been. This was the original indication I received from the officials of my department.

Perhaps during the course of his replies to other questions the minister

will tell us or have his colleague the Secretary of State do so, why this rather extraordinary procedure was adopted. This is an item of the unforeseen kind under the Department of Finance. Why not be straightforward and say this is a special project under the Minister of Labour?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Perhaps I could answer-

If I may finish, this intrigues me a little because frankly the one who is going to be spending the money or to have the authority to spend the money is the Minister of Labour, acting on behalf of other ministers. Why not say so and put it in his own estimates, rather than have this usually minor catch-all provision under the Department of Finance?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I should like to say that I have a great deal of sympathy for the hon. member for Edmonton West, because that was the original idea that was held when this project was first brought forward. I do not want to take refuge behind officials. I was an official once myself, and I always believed that the minister should take responsibility for these things. We were advised that from an administrative point of view it would be easier to do it this way. There is an "unforeseen" vote anyway in the department. I will come to the word "unforeseen" in a minute.
As the hon. member does know, because he has probably attended treasury board meetings assiduously, the amounts that are spent from the unforeseen vote are later charged back to the department concerned, and were the funds in the Department of Labour or any other department this course would mean another administrative process. We were advised that it would be easier administratively. It will be the intention, of course, to have these projects performed by the Department of Public Works or the department of northern affairs or the department under which they would normally come. The Department of Labour comes into the picture by giving a statement that there is enough labour content, that the project is in the right part of the country where the labour shortages are. Otherwise the projects will not be accepted by treasury board.
This is my understanding of the mechanics. The money will be paid out of this vote and then charged back to the appropriate department at a later stage in the financial procedures for accounting to parliament. It is just to conform with the normal mechanics of government. The hon. gentleman will see that because of the phrase "unforeseen" the wording of the vote is expanded so as to indicate that it is not wholly unforeseen. The only unforeseen element in it, as my hon.

friend has just explained, is that he is collecting a list of projects, but we cannot specify the projects until they have gone through scrutiny.
I think hon. members know that the government has not got power to get started on these things unless there is some vote from parliament authorizing it to do so. If we are to take a recess and not come back until the end of September, we would not want to hold up getting these projects ready and organized so that the actual work could start as early as possible in October and toward the beginning of November, when they would really be needed. I think that is the mechanical side of it.
These items will be charged back to the department in the usual course of administration?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes.

Then is it the intention of the government that parliament will be informed of this particular group of projects, rather than having them lumped together with others and then saying, "Oh, yes, we put up a building for the Department of Agriculture, but it appears under the usual construction items in the vote for the Department of Agriculture"?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I will give an undertaking on behalf of the government that either on the main unforeseen vote of the Department of Finance when it comes before the house, or on the vote of the Department of Labour, on the administrative item, whichever seems to be the more convenient and whichever comes at an opportune time, the government will give a full and detailed account of what projects have been selected, the progress that has been made on them, and the amounts involved.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Did I understand the Minister of Labour to say that it has been projected by his officials that they anticipate a higher degree of unemployment this fall?

Mr. Chairman, I replied to the right hon. gentleman who asked me whether my officials had given me any projection of prospects for unemployment, and I said I had no recent projection. However, I told my right hon. friend, and I repeat this subject to confirming it through notes which I have, that shortly after I became Minister of Labour it was indicated to me that the projections at that time were for greater unemployment this fall and possibly next winter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
That is exactly what I thought I heard. I do not want to become contentious today, because everything so far has been
Supply-Finance
in a more courteous vein than in the last few days, but this statement by the minister is of great significance, and accordingly I think I would agree that the way the spending of this money is being projected is probably a very good idea at this stage. Further, the way the matter was projected by the Secretary of State is worthy of consideration.
I do not want to beat a dead horse, but if the projections are in this direction then it seems to me both ministers should use their influence and good offices to get this sales tax measure removed. They would achieve a much higher degree of employment by doing that and would be much more popular throughout the country.
Mr. Chairman-

I do not want to take the floor from my hon. friend, but 1 was asked a question which I had hoped to answer. However, I interrupted my own statement to answer a question put by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition. In connection with the winter works program, which is a separate program from this particular one, I understand it is possible for an application to be made by a province on behalf of an unincorporated municipality.
For example, in certain parts of Newfoundland municipal organizations do not exist in the accepted sense, but upon inquiry I am informed that on at least one occasion it was possible for a province to make an application for assistance under the winter works program, on behalf of an unincorporated region, or an area that was not a municipality in the usual sense. That is the only information I can give to my hon. friend today, but I would be glad to make further inquiries so I could advise him at a later date.

I thank the minister for that explanation, because that has occurred in my constituency where the owners of privately owned irrigation systems have received assistance. There are a number of other bodies waiting to make application, and I will welcome further information.
The only other question I wish to bring again to the minister's attention concerns co-ordination and co-operation among the departments. I have a concrete illustration of officials of the Department of Agriculture urging certain people to increase production by extending and improving their irrigation system. I have proof of other departments telling them not to increase production and saying "Leave your system alone; we are going to flood you out." However, I found that the Department of Labour did give a grant to these very same

Supply-Finance
people, who received this contrawise advice, for the improvement of their irrigation system. I would like the minister to explain what is the co-ordination which makes it possible for three departments to be working in different directions with respect to the application of the winter works program.

I certainly agree with my hon. friend that it is very important that all departments of government co-operate with a view to adjusting and developing their programs, with the problem of unemployment and the creation of further employment in mind. At present there is an interdepartmental committee involved with the development of projects that might be applied under this particular item, and this committee has as its job the reviewing of all departments and the bringing forward of projects that might assist employment.
From that point of view it seems to me that this committee ought to be the vehicle through which the proper co-ordination of departments is achieved for the purpose of creating employment opportunities. I hope this particular emphasis will be increased rather than decreased, because I believe that further progress can be made along those lines. If that is what the hon. member has in mind, then I certainly accept his suggestion and agree with it fully.

I am sure, Mr. Chairman, all hon. members have excellent ideas on how this comparatively small sum of money could be spent, and assist the national economy, but I would like to point out one matter that would be especially valuable to the objective the minister has outlined. It concerns the construction of small tourist wharfs. Recently I put a number of questions on the order paper concerning a program of small docks and launching ramps projected for my own area and, I understand, for most other areas.
The answers I received to those questions indicate that there has been a very serious cut back in this program from what was planned last year. Most of these jobs are small-in that they would cost anywhere from $5,000 to $15,000. Most of them are in small communities, where the navigation for tourists particularly is uppermost in the minds of the local people. They meet most of the essentials the minister outlined; they are small jobs, a large number of which could be carried out with a small amount of money. I urge that a review of the Department of Public Works tourist works program be undertaken when this vote is passed, because I am given to understand that it was cut back very drastically, not at the request of anyone in particular but merely because the money was not available. If this money is

now being made available I should like to see it used in these very useful projects, which have always brought good results to small communities and have created employment because they involve the provision of local labour and materials.

Mr. Chairman, I want to say just a few words on this vote. It seems to me a very unusual request is being put before parliament at this time. We are being asked to sign a blank cheque for $7 million, and we are not told what projects it is for or where those projects are to be located. I think we should know this. We may not agree with the projects or we may not agree with their location. In view of some of the sad experiences of this house recently with regard to government planning and the government then having to back track, and one thing and another, the minister should have come forward with some definite projects which they have in mind. He should tell us what they are and where they are to be located. This situation seems to me to be the same as that of a sales manager going to the manager of the company and saying, "I want $7 million", and when the manager asks him what it is for he says, "I do not know, but I think we will need it".
I think we are being placed in a rather unusual position in being asked to endorse this supplementary expenditure of $7 million. The minister, rather than cutting back the winter works program as he did, would have been better advised to leave it as it was. This in itself would have helped the employment situation quite a bit. I for one, Mr. Chairman, do not like the way in which we are being asked to accept this vote.

Mr. Chairman, I find it very difficult to understand why the minister and the government have not been able to give us more information as to the projects they have in mind. The minister indicated that it is approximately three months since they were advised of the likelihood of an increase in unemployment this winter. Surely during that period some advice could have been received from the departments with regard to projects that were available. If I understood the minister correctly he indicated that there was already a shelf of projects available to be undertaken under this program in the various departments of the government. It may be a nagging thought, but we wonder why something has not been done along that line so the minister could have brought to our attention at this time some of the projects they are thinking of undertaking under the program.
I have one or two questions I would like to ask the minister. I wonder whether any limit

will be placed upon the amounts that will be available for any one project. Another question that might be of interest to the committee is whether there is any particular type of project that will be excluded from this particular grant of money. Perhaps the minister could answer those questions.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask the minister whether any of these projects had been planned prior to his taking over as minister. I would also like to ask him whether there has been any consultation with the provinces with regard to the spending of this money. I suggest to the minister that the great increase in boating demands a larger number of docks than we have at the present time. Some of these docks would be small, but in the building of them-and I could name dozens of places where they are needed-there is a great deal of labour involved. I would ask the minister to discuss with the Department of Public Works those projects that were cut off after having been planned, or which for some reason or other have been shelved, and to reconsider the building of these docks.

Mr. Chairman, the minister seems to be rather vague about the type of projects and works that may be carried out under this $7 million vote. I wonder whether he can give us any definite information as to what the percentage of labour content should be in a construction project that is being considered, to make it eligible to participate under this vote.

Mr. Chairman, there has been reference during this discussion to the amount of $7 million being rather small. It may be, in the light of the problem that some members of the government foresee; but I think we should bear in mind that $7 million of the taxpayers' money is quite a large sum. In fact 30 years ago in my province of Saskatchewan, at which time we had close to the population we now have, that was half the budget. I hope the minister understands that the matters being put forward at this time are being put forward responsibly because of the apparent situation.
I am not quite clear about this and I want to ask the minister one question. Do I understand that this $7 million is desired for projects only in areas that qualify as surplus manpower areas? I am not clear on this point from what has been said so far. I formed that opinion, but some of my colleagues have indicated that this is not so. I am also interested in the matter of labour content, which I think is very important. Also, would the minister tell us whether this is to be
Supply-Finance
solely an expenditure by the federal government, or will any of it be used in sharing programs that will provide employment?
Carried.

Mr. Chairman, may I call it
one o'clock-
Oh, oh.

-because there are two or three other matters here that should be considered. I would ask hon. members opposite not to fret. They are asking us to accept this vote; a new procedure is being followed, and I think we should be quite careful with it. We can continue with it at 2.30.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
It is one o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The house in committee of supply, supplementary estimates (B), Department of Finance, vote No. 50b.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, after conferring with hon. gentlemen opposite at one o'clock it seems there is a feeling that it would be preferable to have more information about this particular vote than it is possible for the government to give at the present time, for reasons which my hon. friend the Minister of Labour gave and which, I think, are well understood to the hon. member for Ontario who formerly occupied that portfolio. The government has no desire whatsoever to ask the committee to accept any vote without adequate information and explanation. As I explained when the vote was introduced, it is not essential that it be passed at this time. It was thought it would be a convenient thing to have it passed because it is for the purpose, and solely for the purpose, of attempting to alleviate the exceptional unemployment which this country unfortunately has experienced for quite a number of years in the winter months. I do not anticipate there will be any shortage of funds before it is necessary for the government to ask once more for interim supply, particularly as I understand it will be necessary to do so as soon as the house resumes on September 30. Therefore I would ask that this item be allowed to stand and that we proceed to the Department of Transport.

If I may say a word before you make your decision, Mr. Chairman, we realize the necessity that something be done during the winter months, as we have done in the

Supply-Transport
past, in order to alleviate the seasonal unemployment experienced. We put forward programs to this end. However, there is just not enough information available to members of this committee at this time for them to pass a definite sum of $7 million for something which may be determined in the future. My understanding is that these projects can be assembled and approved by treasury board and proceeded with, so that there will be no lessening of any attempt to do something about winter unemployment. These projects can be proceeded with, and when this parliament returns in the fall then the Minister of Labour can put forward the $7 million, or probably even more. From the projects listed and their estimated cost I think probably more will be needed, and every member of the committee will be well enough informed to be able to vote with some intelligence upon a sum of money such as has been suggested. So the work can go on and we can pass the estimates when we come back in the fall.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I just want to say one word. I can assure the hon. gentleman from Ontario and the committee generally that the government has no intention of seeking to take any partisan advantage in this matter whatsoever. I have indicated quite clearly that through interim supply the funds will be available which will be required in the meantime. I detect nowhere in the committee any opposition to the objective of this vote, so that I do not think the government should feel inhibited about going ahead with the program. If there is any dissenter in the committee I wish he would speak up, because I think every hon. member of the house is anxious to do everything he can to see that unemployment is reduced as much as possible in the winter months. Therefore the government will assume that getting interim supply next week gives it a mandate to go on with this program which was outlined by my hon. friend the Minister of Labour. Before we ask parliament finally to determine this matter, we will be very happy to let it stand over till more detailed information is available to parliament.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it agreed that vote 50b stands?

Agreed.
Item stands.
1. Departmental administration, $3,388,600.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The committee will now proceed to the consideration of the estimates

of the Department of Transport, vote No. 1, departmental administration. Shall this vote carry?

Mr. Chairman, during the question period today two questions were asked of me. At that time I assumed that the estimates were being called as the first item of business, immediately after the question hour, otherwise I would have answered one of them forthwith. The other one asked for information of which I was not sufficiently sure to give an accurate answer.
As to the question asked by the hon. member for Churchill having to do with the condition of the runways at the airport at The Pas, the situation is that these runways deteriorated very rapidly and present a real problem. At the moment engineers are trying to assess what requires to be done in the matter. There is not much more useful information I can give him at the moment.
As to the other question asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre concerning the ownership of the Tritonica, the owners are Snowberry Shipping Co., Hamilton, Bermuda. That company being a limited company, I do not know who the shareholders are but I have every reason to believe they are not Canadian.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to say a few words on the estimates of the Department of Transport. In my opinion this is one of the more important departments in the federal field, even more so because ever since the report of the Mac-Pherson royal commission was presented to the government it has been apparent that some of the suggestions or recommendations were of such magnitude and of such far reaching significance that it is almost unbelievable they would be implemented.
For instance, in Saskatchewan alone close to 14,000 farms will be affected by railway abandonment. More than 1,274 miles of railroad are likely to be abandoned and approximately 156 towns would be directly involved. In addition, 318 grain elevators would be put out of commission. All this presents a most serious problem as far as Saskatchewan is concerned. It was said at the turn of the century that if Canada was to take her proper place in the world, her commerce must be increased. The way of bringing this state of affairs about was to build these railroads so that grain could be transferred at low cost to foreign markets. The same basic situation prevails. The grain will still have to be brought to the seaports and if these railroads are abandoned, many farmers, in future, will not be able to deliver their grain.
There may be justification for abandoning some rail lines which run parallel to others,

say 15 miles apart. But if communities are left 50 or 60 miles from the nearest railroad, farmers are going to be hurt very badly. The benefits of the Crowsnest pass rates would disappear. This is a problem which cannot be handed to the transport commissioners for them to solve. It will have to be tackled as a matter of government policy. The government will have to see that these places are not left without a railroad service.
A few days ago I placed a bill before this house seeking to have a grain terminal built at Tisdale in an area which, in the past, could never deliver the same amount of grain as other areas in Saskatchewan. One purpose of my bill was to enable shipments to be expedited through Port Churchill. Should these abandonment proposals go through, the three western provinces would, I think, need many new terminals. In former years when there was a surplus of grain the federal government had to pay as much as $50 million in storage charges to the grain companies. A terminal built by the government would cost approximately $2 per bushel stored, a cost of, say, $10 million. In years of surplus the government would not have to pay for storage in federally-owned elevators and this saving would, in itself, justify building such terminals as I have proposed. It has been said that private companies would provide storage on railroads which have not been abandoned. This might be so, but some of these places could easily be 50 or 60 miles away from the farmer concerned. If it were not economic for private companies to build grain elevators at such places, then government terminals should be built.
It was thought by some people when I introduced my bill that this was an exaggerated idea and that the government could not build these inland terminals. But in the light of the fact that as many as 15,500 people might be affected, it is not hard to see that a time may be coming when governments will have to start building these publicly-owned terminals.
I know the minister is anxious to get his estimates passed and I do not want to elaborate on what I have said because I did present the case on an earlier occasion. At the same time I would urge the hon. gentleman to see that the abandonment of railway lines is not left for some such body as the board of transport commissioners alone to deal with. The government itself must outline a program to see that the farmers will not be deprived of their privileges, deprived of the benefit of the Crowsnest pass rates and deprived of the opportunity to get their grain to market as cheaply and efficiently as possible.
Supply-Transport

I should like to congratulate the hon. gentleman on his appointment as Minister of Transport, one of the more important departments of government and one of particular interest to western Canada, especially at this time, for reasons which have just been given by my hon. friend from Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale in his comments on rail line abandonment.
We in western Canada know there are some lines which will have to be abandoned because of economic reasons. At the same time we want to be sure that such abandonment as may take place does not in any way cut into the benefits now enjoyed by farmers in western Canada under the Crowsnest pass rates agreement. I wish to underline this statement because some of the intentions which have recently come to light indicate that the railways are not taking into consideration the long distances some farmers will have to cover in order to get their produce to the rail lines which remain in existence. I was greatly heartened by the minister's statement this morning during the question period when he indicated these were only intentions, and that many of these lines would not necessarily be abandoned in the period that lies ahead.
Another matter that is requiring a great deal of consideration at the present time is the continuing of the program for the elimination of grade crossings. As all hon. members know, during the past several years quite a problem has developed in the vicinity of many of our towns because of the use of diesel engines, in that sometimes there will be three or four engines pulling as many as 200 cars. It is a difficult problem both for the crew of the train and the people wishing to use the crossing. I urge the minister and the government to consider a greatly expanded program for the elimination of these crossings by providing underpasses or overpasses, whichever may be suitable. This might be one of the programs that might be undertaken in connection with the item that has just been allowed to stand.
There is another matter that comes under the Department of Transport in which there is a great deal of interest in my area. I refer to the provision of airstrips for private aircraft. Many people are looking to the government to provide greater assistance than in the past, in order to facilitate the development of transportation by this means. A greater number of people are purchasing their own aircraft, and many more would do so for their private use if they were assured that municipalities could secure some assistance in the provision of suitable airstrips. There are a number of other things I will

Supply-Transport
deal with when we are discussing the individual items, but that is all I wish to say at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I should say something at this point, since the remarks pertaining to the railways are of a general nature and not specifically dealt with as such. I thank hon. members who have just spoken for their kind references to the department. There is one thing I think I should say about the remarks of the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale, in which he set out absolute figures as to the numbers of elevators involved in the abandonment of railways lines. I wish to warn against anyone accepting such figures as absolute because we do not yet know what lines, or what mileages are involved in any possible program of abandonment. Therefore any figures given now might very well prove to be inaccurate.
Hon. members are perfectly correct in describing the problem as one of very great importance to the prairie provinces. There is no doubt about that at all, and I do not think anyone is more willing to recognize that fact than I am. The situation is simply that in 1959, presumably because of the complexities of the problem, the former government appointed the MacPherson royal commission to examine railway transportation matters. The committee finally made a report and no action was taken before the former government left office. In fairness, however, I must say there is every indication that they were seeking to take action and had legislation on the subject in the course of preparation, although that legislation was never in any way made public.
Since taking office the present government has given a great deal of attention to this matter. As I indicated in my opening remarks on the estimates, the legislation on the subject which I hope to bring before this session of parliament is complex and difficult. On two major points it would involve some difference in thinking from what I take to be the position of the former government. That can be explained however either on the basis of a difference in point of view or as the result of further examination of a very difficult and complex subject. In any event, there is the clearest possible recognition of the fact that what is needed is to rationalize any program of rail abandonment, to coordinate it and carry it out in such a way as to result in the minimum of adverse consequences in the areas concerned. That is the purpose of the legislation.
It is not proper for me to anticipate at this time legislation not yet before the house, but in order to allay any misconceptions or
[Mr. Nasserden.l
undue fears about it I think I should give some indication of what our thinking is in preparing the legislation. Legislation is being prepared in close co-operation with the prairie provinces and the maritime provinces, these provinces being more directly concerned, and after consideration of the many representations received from some of the provincial premiers and their officials in the provincial departments dealing with this subject. I hope that when we have the legislation ready for submission to the house it will reflect adequate consideration of their points of view, and the great knowledge they have of this subject because of their concern with railway problems over the years.
There are, of course, other recommendations of tremendous importance in the MacPherson commission report which deal with the methods of setting freight rates. I am not unaware of the complexity of this subject and I hope I am not unaware of the things that will have to be avoided in bringing in new legislation on the subject. I thought I should make these remarks at this stage so that there would be no undue fear on the part of members or the people in the areas vitally concerned with this problem.

May I ask the minister a question on this very subject? In answer to a question on the orders of the day this morning he stated that the government had formed a cabinet committee to deal with branch line abandonments, and that this was in accordance with an election promise of the Prime Minister. We had a similar cabinet committee in the past when we were in office. That committee met with the premiers of the provinces to discuss this very subject and also had an opportunity to discuss it with officials of the provincial governments and other interested ministers. Can the minister tell us if the cabinet committee of the present government has had meetings with the premiers of the prairie provinces on the matter of branch line abandonment?

The meetings were conducted on an individual basis, not with the premiers collectively, and the form of meeting varied with the different provinces. In the case of Alberta I met with the premier and the provincial government agent alone. Then the officials continued to work on it at their level. In the case of Saskatchewan my colleagues and I on the transportation committee met with the premier of the province and a delegation. In the case of the province of Nova Scotia I may have been alone; I am not sure. Two representatives of the maritimes commission, I believe, were there as well. Then, in the case of Manitoba, I did not meet with

the premier, but what he described as I believe his working team of experts from the government met with the officials of the department. This has been done in other areas with the premiers concerned.
In other words I thought that because railway problems vary from province to province, it would be more effective to meet the provincial representatives individually, rather than meet a collective group. One province will be more concerned with one aspect of railway problems than another. I would not want it to be thought that the only railway problems discussed were those related to railway line abandonment. Problems inherent in rate making and things of that sort were also discussed at some length.

I gather from what the minister has said that the great plan announced by the Prime Minister during the election concerning this commission of the federal government to meet with the interested provinces has not materialized so far. The minister has been meeting from time to time with representatives of the provinces and the new government has been doing less, so far as talks with the provinces are concerned, than was being done under the old government?

No, Mr. Chairman, that would be a completely wrong assessment of the situation. I took the trouble, when starting into this subject, to check as closely as I could on what had been done by the former government in this area. I cannot speak for the former government. I can only say what I found when I took over and what information could be obtained from records and talking with people who were there at the meetings. The procedure we have adopted is the converse of that situation under the former government.
As I understand it, the former government confronted the provinces with proposals for legislation that were a fait accompli. The provinces were confronted collectively. What I have been seeking to do is the very opposite. In working this plan out-and we have tried to be very careful because I think it is of vital importance to the provinces-we tried to arrive at a plan that would meet the wishes of the provinces and other organizations as well, such as the wheat pools and others. We have brought them in to get their ideas, to discuss the kind of legislation that they think will meet the problems as they see them. While it is quite true we will have to take responsibility for the legislation, it should be legislation prepared as a result of consideration of the arguments that these representatives put forward. Furthermore, we are following this up by having the working people
Supply-Transport
of the department at the technical level follow the consultations through.
I am hoping that in this complex and difficult subject we will get better results in the end. In saying that, I do not mean to imply criticism of the former government in that respect. I must say that this method of proceeding was worked out while having the benefit of knowing how the former government had proceeded, and having the opportunity of deciding what I thought could be improvement in the method of dealing with the provinces on this point.
I do not want the minister to leave this impression-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; I recognized the hon. member for Churchill.

There are several points I should like to bring to the attention of the minister while we are discussing item 1 of the estimates of this department. First of all, I should like to refer to the minister's reply concerning the condition of the runways at The Pas, Manitoba. I appreciate the information that the engineers are looking over these runways in an endeavour to see what can be done. I know the people will be gratified with this information. I understand also that since they are making this investigation we can be reasonably sure every effort will be made by them to turn in a report on the work which is necessary. However, I am hoping that, when it is proven this work is necessary, there will be no hold-up along the line anywhere. This is extremely important, not only to the people of The Pas but to various people in all parts of northern Manitoba.
The aircraft which has been making the regular scheduled flights into The Pas, as I mentioned this morning, was a Viscount, but it is unable to land at The Pas. The company that operates this service has inaugurated a shuttle service with DC-3's between Thompson and other points in the north, bringing passengers from those points into Flin Flon. They are just coping with the situation on a temporary basis, but that is disrupting many things right at The Pas airport.
As the minister probably knows, this airport was constructed somewhere around 1942, and was taken over by the Department of Transport at a later date. Since then, industry has built up in northern Manitoba and several small businesses have sprung up in the area of The Pas airport as a result of the increase in passenger services. If something is not done to have these services resumed as quickly as possible, these people are also going to suffer considerable financial loss. I would hope, therefore, the minister

Supply-Transport
would seriously consider this report when it is available and take the appropriate action as quickly as possible.
There is another airport in northern Manitoba which is extremely important, namely the one at Thompson, Manitoba. I understand that plans are under way for the hard surfacing of the runways at this airport. I ask for the utmost co-operation from the minister in seeing that there are no road blocks put in the way of this work going ahead as rapidly as possible. I do not know what the situation is at the present time. However, the last time I inquired it was hoped the hard surfacing could begin this year, and I sincerely hope that will be the case.
My congratulations go out to the officials of the minister's department for the very splendid work they have carried out on airstrips in northern Manitoba in recent years. At both Flin Flon and Lynn Lake we have new 5,000 foot runways, forming part of a network of airways throughout northern Canada. These strips are widely used and appreciated by the people of the area. They are a credit to the department, and I can assure the minister that the planning and engineering which went into them left nothing to be desired. Both the headquarters staff and regional staff at Winnipeg worked in close co-operation in doing this work.
However there is one thing which does create a problem for the local authorities in the operating and maintenance of these airstrips. It is a problem well known to the officials of the department, that which local authorities have of finding enough money to operate the strips.
I know there are regulations under which subsidies are granted, and in the case of Flin Flon everyone is quite happy with the type of system that is in effect. In fact, much to the surprise of some people, I believe they have found it economically profitable to operate the airport there. As against that there are places like Lynn Lake which have repeatedly sought, and in some cases received, assistance in the form of snow removal equipment for the maintenance of runways. This is a bigger item than a lot of people realize because the runways must be maintained in perfect condition throughout the winter. Snow removal must be kept up almost daily and it becomes very expensive.
I would ask the minister to give this problem his utmost consideration, and when requests of this nature come in I would ask that he send recommendations to the officials concerned to co-operate in every possible way.
I have found that many small places in the north which have local airstrips also have very ambitious flying clubs which provide
fMr. Simpson.]
good community service to adjacent areas. These clubs in many cases are desperately in need of some sort of assistance, and I do not know where else they can get it except from the department. However, from inquiries which I have made, I have discovered that the regulations do not permit the department to grant some of the assistance which has been requested.
As an example I mention Swan River in Manitoba, where on many occasions members of the local flying club have in emergencies flown patients out to various hospitals, and have provided other public services to the community. The club has been requesting the department to supply it with a temporary lighting kit so that the airfield, when necessary, could be used for night flying. But the regulations do not permit the department to supply any equipment of that nature to anything other than a municipally administered airport, or to a Department of Transport airport. This is something which should be examined so that if by chance the department has surplus equipment of this kind it could be made available to recognized and authorized flying clubs, on either a loan or rental basis, as the department may see fit.
This is very important as such clubs cannot expect too much aid from municipalities. They are not costing the treasury of Canada anything, and small requests of this nature should be met if at all possible.
There is only one other matter I wish to mention, and I shall be brief because I understand the hon. member for the Northwest Territories has something to say about it. It has been suggested to me on many occasions, particularly in the north, that the possibility be examined of providing, under conditions set out by the department, some search and rescue, or homing equipment for private aircraft operating in the northern areas.
Hon. members who represent northern constituencies have from time to time experienced the anxiety, and in many cases the tragedy, of planes going down in the bush-land. In many cases long searches are necessary before these planes and the survivors, if any, are found. Many of the bush flyers have brought it to my attention that if this equipment were installed on their airplanes very little time would be lost in finding the wreckage if they were forced down. However the small operators feel this equipment is a little too expensive.
One of the main items of expense arises from the fact that the batteries are costly and do not last very long. However I understand that many of these so called SARAH sets are available, and if the Department of Transport could compel all pilots flying in

designated areas to have this equipment, and further, could supply it to them on a loan basis, we might find that the savings which would result from the money now spent on air search and rescue would be sufficient to cover a plan of this nature.
In conclusion I would like to mention rail transportation. I shall not deal with the freight rate situation, as I dealt with this some weeks ago when speaking in the house on the desirability of equalization of freight rates. At that time there was some opposition from the parties to my left because I did not offer any concrete solution for the problem, but I did point out that it was gone into very thoroughly by the MacPherson royal commission, and I said certain of its recommendations should be examined closely.
In my area there is little highway competition for the Canadian National Railways, and in practically every place where there is no competition from highway traffic there is no free pickup and delivery of express or l.c.l. freight. The moment the road goes in, the railway generally puts in a system of free pickup and delivery of express and l.c.l. freight. I think this is a matter that should be looked into by the minister so that all points served by Canadian National Railways receive the same consideration in this regard.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few moments to bring to the attention of the minister an airport problem concerning the greater Vancouver area. Before I do that, my colleague the hon. member for Port Arthur, who is not here this afternoon, asked me to ask the minister when he may expect a specific answer to his question No. 963 on the order paper.
In recent years the air traffic at the Vancouver international airport has become such that there has been a move to remove the smaller, light aircraft away from that very busy airport. With this object in mind, a few years ago a new airport site was selected for light aircraft at a place called Pitt Meadows about 25 miles from Vancouver. The site is not a very good one in the view of many people. The body charged with regional planning for that area of British Columbia, the lower mainland regional planning board, specifically recommended against the choice of this site for more than one reason. They felt it was not a good site for aircraft and it would be spoiling an otherwise good industrial site. The minister has recognized the fact that it is not a very good site. He was out there last week to open this new, light aircraft airport, and this is the report contained in the Vancouver Province of July 22 in connection with that visit:
Supply-Transport
Transport minister George Mcllraith said before the opening ceremonies that he did not know why Pitt Meadows was chosen for an airport.
''It was one of the things I inherited from the last government", he said.
The light aircraft operators are divided on this topic. One group has moved to the new airport and another group, the B.C. aircraft owners and pilots association, has refused to move. There is another airport available in the area. This is at Boundary Bay, British Columbia, which was built during the war as an air force training airport. It is a very large site. In recent years it has been used as a wireless station by the Department of National Defence. The light aircraft association has asked the Department of National Defence if they will give up part of this site -it is no longer used as an airport-for the use of light aircraft. It is much more handy to the main population centre and I believe it has much less rainfall than the site at Pitt Meadows. The Department of National Defence have replied that they cannot give this site up, for security reasons, because this wireless station is supposed to be so very secure. In order to test the security of this installation the Vancouver Province newspaper sent two reporters out there. They were allowed past the gate without giving in a pass. They drove around this supposedly secure place. They took pictures. They drove at 60 miles per hour on runways, and they eventually left without giving in a pass. The matter was brought to the attention of the Department of National Defence and the commissionaire on the gate was fired. However, the reporters made the point that civilians go in and out all the time and that just a mile from there is a small, private airfield with 25 aircraft which fly over this site all the time. The point, of course, is that it really does not need to be so secure as the Department of National Defence would have us believe.
The B.C. aircraft owners and pilots association have suggested to the Department of National Defence that some arrangement could be made whereby this site could be used both for the wireless station and by the light aircraft owners. I realize that this involves the Department of National Defence, but it also involves the Department of Transport and I hope the minister will speak to his colleague about this matter at some time. The Vancouver Province of July 16 summarized the situation in this way, in question and answer form, putting forth the views of the Department of National Defence and those of the light aircraft owners:
Here are the arguments:
Government: It would cost too much money to move the installation at Boundary Bay and a better site is not available anyway.

Supp ly-Transport
Pilots: Don't move it; there are 825 acres and lots of room for both of us. Just fence it at our expense.
Government: The runways are in bad condition and not suitable for landing small aircraft.
Pilots: The runways are excellent, once a few weeds have been removed.
This resulted from the testimony of the reporters who looked at it:
Government: The small aircraft would represent a threat to national security; it is a wireless station-not an airport.
Pilots: It has always been an airport and the presence of a public skating rink, and hundreds of civilians has not been termed a risk up to now.
Government: The flight of small aircraft will cause an electrical disturbance that will interfere with the wireless operation.
Pilots: There are 27 aircraft based about a mile away and have been for some time. The field is in the flight paths of a great deal of activity from Vancouver airport and the Seattle-Tacoma airport.
Government: There is too much fog at Boundary Bay and the weather conditions are not as good as at Pitt Meadows.
Pilots: There is far less fog at Boundary Bay; Ladner nearby gets only 36.23 inches of rain a year as compared to 88.94 inches at Pitt Polder near Pitt Meadows.
What makes this a rather important problem in our area is that the lower mainland of British Columbia is a relatively land poor area. It is surrounded by mountains, the ocean and includes the United States border, and there is not very much land. This site would, I am sure, make an excellent site for light aircraft. The people who use these aircraft generally live in the metropolitan area. They would not have so far to travel, and the site is a better one from the point of view of weather.
I would conclude my remarks by appealing to the minister to consult with his officials and with his colleague the Minister of National Defence to see whether the two positions cannot be reconciled. The light aircraft owners have suggested a means whereby the wireless station could be fenced and made perfectly secure, and the runways could be used by the light aircraft owners. I would hope the minister will give this matter some consideration and speak to the Minister of National Defence about it.

Mr. Chairman, what I have to say concerns what was discussed a little earlier, the question of railway line abandonment. This is a matter which is not on nearly as large a scale in my area as it is in western Canada, but it is none the less important to us in the east. At the present there is an application before the board of transport commissioners to abandon about 25 miles of railway line between the villages of Tata-magouche in the constituency of Colchester-Hants and Scotsburn in the constituency of my colleague the hon. member for Pictou. This
