rail line abandonment would isolate some communities on that north shore, and-and this is important-it will isolate a farmers' co-operative which deals in western feed grains.
Also of great significance is the fact that this line connecting, as it does, Oxford and Stellarton, provides an alternate route into the province of Nova Scotia. Although it is not of the standard of a main line, it has been used on many occasions as an emergency route when there has been a blockage of the main line. In the last few days there was a serious derailment on the main line and according to press reports passenger traffic was routed over this alternate route. If this abandonment is allowed it will remove 25 miles from the centre of this line and will break this link. I think it is rather important to remember that not only would this link serve southern and eastern Nova Scotia in an emergency, but it would also connect the routes leading into Newfoundland. I might add I noted yesterday that the municipal council of Colchester county endorsed a resolution opposing this abandonment. I just wanted to bring this matter to the attention of the minister so that when consideration is given to the over-all problem of rail line abandonment he will also consider this question, not only in the light in which it is held locally but also having in mind the fact that it is an alternative route into that part of the country.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps I might answer one or two of these questions now, and I will try to do so as concisely as possible. One matter I forgot to mention to the hon. member for Three Rivers is that the committee on transportation, now in full operation, meets, I think, what was put forward by the Prime Minister in the election campaign. I did examine the point quite carefully and am satisfied about that.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond raised the point about the satellite air station at the international airport at Vancouver. The problem there is quite simple. There is a great deal of traffic involving large aircraft coming into Vancouver airport. The take-offs and landings of small aircraft which use the satellite airport have been as high as 620 in a single day, so that the hon. member can see the need for taking action. The former government did take action, it is true, but I did not want to take the responsibility for the accuracy of the report in the Vancouver Province because I have not seen the report. It may or it may not be accurate. I did mention the subject when opening Pitt Meadows airport on Saturday, but I do not recall any reference to the

subject mentioned by the hon. member. He referred to light aircraft. Great numbers of these light aircraft people are very enthusiastic and keen about the Pitt Meadows airport. The small aircraft owners association, headed by a gentleman, who I think I can say without impropriety, was rather vocal on the subject, for some reason refuse to accept the simple statement of fact that it is not possible to have the military air base at Boundary Bay vacated for use as a statellite airport. That is not possible. I tried to make that point clear in all interviews, whether with the press or the radio and television people, in Vancouver on Saturday. Flying into that airport and using only part of the field, and so on, is not possible. The unfortunate part of it is that the Department of National Defence has not been able to give as fully as it might wish, the reason it is not possible to make this airport available; I think I should make that clear.
While I said it is quite true that the Pitt Meadows airport was chosen by the former government and work was undertaken on it, I can see nothing in the files which would lead me to believe other than that there was very careful consideration of the alternative. The other alternative was to locate in an area where there are a great number of residents, and the university there would have been interfered with rather seriously. I am sorry that this lack of understanding about the non-availability of Boundary Bay airport has not been made clear before, and I hope my remarks today will tend to provide an appreciation of that point.
As to the reference to distance with regard to the Pitt Meadows airport, as the hon. member knows from living in the area, there are new road construction programs under way in Vancouver. Accessibility to the airport from the centre of the city on the new roads I am sure will be much better than the accessibility of the airport with the existing roads today.
The hon. member for Colchester-Hants made reference to rail line abandonment in his particular area. I have to confess that I simply have no knowledge of that particular abandonment, and I would be less than frank if I said otherwise. But I can tell him that I am a little partial to his part of the country and I would like to make a personal inspection of it one of these days. I could think of nothing more pleasant. In any event the matter is before the board of transport commissioners at the present time, and I hope he has made his point of view clear in the appropriate way.
Another hon. member asked me about a question on the order paper; I have forgot-
Supply-Transport
ten the number. I expect the answer to that rather lengthy question to be available next week.
The hon. member for Churchill asked about the Thompson airport and the paving contract. The tender call for that will be going out next week.

Mr. Chairman, the few observations I have to make this afternoon might be more properly made at a hearing on bilingualism and biculturalism, but since they concern more particularly the C.N.R., I shall make them now.
As the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcll-raith) is aware, I have exchanged a few letters with him where I suggested to give a more bilingual character to the administration and the operation of the railway. In fact, I think we could use the national railways as a means to promote bilingualism all across Canada.
But, when you travel by C.N.R., you are forcefully made aware of the fact that you are entering wagons which are owned by only one group of the population and I think that the use of a little more French besides English would further the cause of bilingualism. If he did that, the minister would create quite a reputation for himself as champion of that cause, and some of the honour would be reflected on his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Cantin) who could claim also some credit for himself.
In the answers the minister sent me, I found nothing to show that my suggestions would be welcome. And if I raise the matter in the house, it is because I think the minister answered in such vague terms that I cannot know whether the responsible authorities will take them into consideration.
In fact, if I refer to the letter the minister wrote me on June 17, 1963, here is what I find:
Be assured that I will be glad to take it up with the management of the company right away.
And in his letter of July 3, 1963, the minister told me:
Be assured that I immediately brought to the attention of the management of the company your additional remarks.
Mr. Chairman, what I would like to know from the minister is whether he has given instructions or whether he intends to give any to the appropriate authorities of the Canadian National Railways in order that, in

Supply-Transport
the future, posters, boards and signs be written in both French and English, in the stations and on the C.N.R. cars.
It seems most abnormal, for instance, to see in all C.N.R. stations in the province of Quebec signs and posters in English only; since the present government has decided to create a royal commission on bilingualism and biculturalism, I believe that it has a wonderful opportunity to give convincing concrete evidence of its desire to take action.
In addition, I say once more to the minister that he would acquire an enviable reputation for himself and for his parliamentary secretary if he acted in furtherance of the various suggestions I made to him.

In view of the fact that I have the honour to represent the largest railway terminal in Canada on a per capita basis I feel that I should draw a few matters to the attention of the minister. First of all, I should like to express my thanks and appreciation for the fine co-operation I received from the hon. gentleman's predecessor, the minister of transport in the former government. He was always most genial and kind and he understood my many problems.
During his period in office we discussed, among many other things, the lengthening of the runways at Moncton airport and I was given to understand that they would be lengthened this year. However, I am afraid that provision for this will not appear in the estimates. Moncton airport is one of the largest in Canada on the basis of arrivals and departures. It is my understanding that we rank eighth. It was clearly brought home to us not long ago, however, that modern facilities at Moncton are sadly lacking. We had arranged a board of trade mission to the old country and it was necessary for us to leave from the city of Halifax because the airstrip at Moncton was not adequate to handle DC-8 aircraft. I bring this to the attention of the minister because this airport serves not only Moncton and the surrounding area but also, to a large degree, the province of Prince Edward Island as far as air travel is concerned.
Our terminal facilities are antiquated. They are not in keeping with today's standards. The minister has told me that some effort will be made to deal with this in 1964. Restaurant facilities are in another building and passengers are called upon to climb several flights of stairs before they can get coffee or a meal. This is certainly not the situation in other parts of Canada, and it should not be the case at an airport such as Moncton, having regard to the volume of business which is done there.
Now I should like to say a few words about the Canadian National Railways, because we have some 7,000 employees of the Canadian National in my constituency. I know we are all very much interested in employment at this time. I have taken note of the overtures made by the city of Winnipeg concerning the removal of terminal maintenance facilities from Winnipeg to Montreal. I should like to protest a move which took place some three years ago which resulted in our Canadian National passenger car shop going from Moncton to Winnipeg, closing out our entire operation in this regard. Fifteen years ago we had about 3,000 people working in our main shop. Now we have about 850. I should like to draw the attention of the minister to the importance of having this shop reopened. Passenger traffic has increased by 250 per cent in the Atlantic region and this work should be done in Moncton. It would not only be good for employment there but it would mean a saving to the C.N.R. of the cost involved in transporting equipment to Winnipeg and then returning it to Moncton for service.
Another matter I should like to mention concerns the contract entered into by the C.N.R. under which the company was to develop 25 acres on Moncton's main street. This work was to be completed by June 1, 1963. There has already been built, and I commend those responsible, an eight storey palatial office building in Moncton which certainly is a credit to our city. But when is this $15 million development project to go forward? Work on this project has been stopped without any reason being given. People in my constituency are continually asking me when it will go forward or whether a hitch has occurred in the plan. No distinct stand seems to have been taken by the railway company. Work has been started on the C.N.R. station. I have received protests from the city council to the effect that this station is far too small and that it will not accommodate the present passenger traffic, let alone the traffic which they expect in the future.
A number of hon. members on the other side have spoken about rail abandonment proposals. Perhaps to a lesser degree, we in the maritime provinces have a similar problem. In some cases the abandonment of lines may be necessary but I feel that in others the board of transport commissioners are too hasty in approving abandonment proposals. I do not think there is any doubt that the board is pro-railway. They go out and hold hearings. Then they come back to Ottawa and pontificate. They say: "Yes, you had' better abandon that line". It all seems a form they run through. The line is abandoned, many people are put out of work and commerce is in some cases reduced to a standstill.

I am sorry the hon. member for Port Arthur is not here today. He referred to me a couple of weeks ago in the course of some comments he had to make about the morale of railway workers. I have to agree with him that it is not as it should be. This is not due to top management but rather to the fact that in some cases men with 25 or 30 years service have been laid off. This is not a good situation. Hence we have bills coming before this house saying that people who have been hurt in this way should receive compensation.
I know of no finer way in which to relieve unemployment than to use this crown corporation. It is fairly well organized and has been going on for a great number of years. There are many avenues in the lumber industry and in other industries across Canada that are yet untouched and which Canadian National Railways could assist in developing. If we are going to close down railway lines all the time in this young country of ours it is a very great mistake. We have found that out already in many cases. In some cases where lines have been abandoned it has been revealed later that they never should have been closed down. However, the railways will not admit this. These are a few of the smaller items that I should like to draw to the attention of the minister.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this item I feel I do so from a good position, because I am the representative of a constituency of 1,300,000 square miles, give or take 50,000 or 60,000, roughly the size of the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia put together. I mention this because if the Northwest Territories have anything in real abundance it is distance, and this has tremendous implications for the future development of the aviation industry in the Northwest Territories. In my view the Minister of Transport has an opportunity to play a vital role in assisting in the development of the 40 per cent of Canada that lies north of the 60th parallel.
At the present time almost all phases of development in the Canadian north are directly dependant on aircraft. The great surge of northern development occurred in the wake of the use of aircraft. It is probably true to say that every producing mine in the Northwest Territories owes its existence to the fact that aircraft were available initially to take in prospectors to remote areas and then played a vital and continuing role during the construction and operation phases of all mining communities in the north.
In terms of government services, and the minister is well aware they have been expanded many times over during the past five
Supply-Transport
or six years, every one of our major services in the north is directly dependant upon aircraft. Our health services are dependant on aircraft for the transportation of hundreds of people from the remote areas of the constituency to larger centres for medical treatment. Our educational system in the Northwest Territories is dependant on aircraft to be able to move hundreds of children thousands of miles each fall into the larger centres where there are schools, and to return them home in the spring for their summer holidays. Government administration could not be carried on in the Canadian north without aircraft.
I have risen at this time to ask the minister a few questions in relation to aircraft. The first thing to which I should like to refer is a matter that was raised by the Minister of National Defence relating to the partial closing down of the distant early warning line in the far north. The closure of some of these sites raises the question of alternative uses. I think it also points up that the writing is on the wall so far as the remainder of the distant early warning line is concerned. I hope that the Minister of Transport will be in continuing consultation with the Minister of National Defence with regard to alternative use of the hanger facilities and refueling and telecommunication facilities that the distant early warning line could provide for commercial operators who are attempting to provide service in the far north.
I would be interested in having the minister tell me something about his plans for airports. Many northern communities are at present cut off from all medical and other supplies for almost four months of the year during the periods of freeze-up in the fall and break-up in the spring. In 1963, when it is possible to send a cosmonaut in orbit around the world in one day, then send up a girl to find out how he is doing and retrieve both of them safely several days later within a few yards of waiting newsmen, I find it inconceivable that thousands of our northern Canadian citizens should be in precarious isolation for 25 per cent of the year.
I suggest to the minister that a massive program of airport development is now required for the far north. I am not referring to paved runways with strobe lights. I am talking about smaller emergency type strips adjacent to the 20 or 30 northern communities that have absolutely no airport facilities whatsoever at the present time. I would hope that the Minister of Transport would also be in close consultation with the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources with a view to co-ordinating work projects in the north to provide these emergency airstrips.

Supply-Transport
I should like the minister to support an increased program of aids to navigation. By this I mean nothing more than the provision of navigational beacons. I should like to give the minister one example of what I have in mind. During the spring campaign I had occasion to fly in a single engine aircraft from Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, 600 miles due east to Baker Lake, Northwest Territories. The present aids to navigation in that entire 600 mile trip consist of the Thelon river which has been there many thousands of years. The position of travellers in the Canadian north, who quite frequently go on trips that take them thousands of miles, is rendered that much more insecure and unsafe by the failure to provide adequate aids to navigation. I would hope that the minister would have the appropriate section of his department look into the possibilities of providing better service to the bush pilots by making available information on such things as upper atmosphere winds.
A matter that is, perhaps oddly enough, of immediate concern to those of us who make our homes in the western part of the Canadian north is the fate of the municipal airport at Edmonton. I would hope that the minister's department could clear up this matter rather quickly. As he may be aware, those people who live along the Mackenzie river depend almost entirely on the service provided by Pacific Western Airlines flights to bring them mail and supplies. It is important to Pacific Western Airlines and therefore to the people of the north that the municipal airport in the heart of downtown Edmonton be available. It is important to us, because we depend on arrangements for the transportation of supplies on a daily basis to Pacific Western Airlines at the municipal airport for furtherance to the north. We consider that any move to Nisku airport would increase the costs of freight handling for us. We know for certain it would be much more inconvenient.
I should like to have the minister tell us something about the plans of his department for the provision of safety equipment for commercial operators in the Northwest Territories. Some time ago I received a return to a question concerning the cost of R.C.A.F. search and rescue operations in the Northwest Territories. The total cost in 1962 was well over $250,000. I predict that in 1963, R.C.A.F. search and rescue costs in the Northwest Territories alone will exceed $1 million. It seems to me that the Department of Transport must examine this very carefully to find if there might be a way of not only providing commercial operators in the far north with safer equipment in terms of rendering air travel more secure, but also in terms of saving the Canadian taxpayer a good many dollars.

I also raised a question some time ago about the firefighting equipment available at those air terminals that are in existence along the Mackenzie river. The answer I received was that the standard of equipment at these airports was not adequate to meet the minimum standards of the department, but that the department would look into it. I hope this situation can be corrected immediately, especially at a time when Pacific Western Airlines, who serves the western part of the north, are providing DC-6 service on a daily basis to many of our northern communities. We would hope the department would take immediate steps to provide the kind of firefighting equipment necessary at the terminals at which these aircraft arrive.
In closing, Mr. Chairman, I want to make a passing reference to the resignation of Mr. Paul Davoud, who was chairman of the air transport board and who was known by a great many northerners. We notice his resignation with some regret. His efforts as chairman of the air transport board were appreciated by everyone who was interested in northern Canada. We hope his successor will bring to the position the same kind of enthusiasm and effort to a very demanding job.

Mr. Chairman, I should like first to congratulate the minister upon his appointment and to thank him for his prompt attention to any matter I have brought to his notice. I should like also to say I appreciate the co-operation and good work of the permanent senior officials in Ottawa and throughout the country. I might say these gentlemen carry on the administration of this department behind the scenes. They are like flowers that bloom unseen and waste their sweetness on the desert air. Frequently I have to deal with matters of national and international scope, but this afternoon, because of the nature of these estimates and the type of constituency I represent, I will apologize, Mr. Chairman, if you think on occasion I am somewhat parochial.
I am going to deal with my complaints in sequence because I think the minister can deal with them better under these circumstances, and this method avoids interruption when the items arise. The first matter I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is the question of continued passenger service on the Kettle Valley Railway. I have mentioned it on previous occasions in this house. I continue to receive letters in this respect from chambers of commerce, trade unions, women's organizations, and boards of trade, and they all say, "Whatever you do, Bert, don't give up on the Kettle Valley Railway." So, I am raising this matter.
I wish to bring to the minister's attention certain changed circumstances that have to

be considered by the board of transport commissioners when they are giving consideration to the application of the Canadian Pacific for the withdrawal of this service. I have a letter here from the local chairman of the brotherhood of railway trainmen. I should like to quote from one paragraph, because this information changes the whole circumstances and removes the reason given for changing the service some years ago. This information removes the argument advanced by the Canadian Pacific at that time. In so far as the financial argument is concerned, if the company would not divorce the passenger service receipts from the revenues of the company as a whole, this is one of the most profitable lines in Canada. The company is located in an area which returns the greatest profit to the C.P.R. because of its association with Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. I quote the following paragraph from the letter from W. H. To whey:
The R.C.M.P. have taken off all railroad bridge guards and the C.P.R. will have all walking track patrols taken off by August 15, 1963. This means that after August 15,	1963, the areas between
Nelson, Midway and Trail will be back to the normal police protection, the same as it was back in 1952. There will be no rail bridge guards or track guards or patrols night or day.
In other words, Mr. Chairman, this means we have returned to normal in Kootenay West so far as railway traffic operations are concerned and the hazards that were related thereto. I do hope the board of transport commissioners will give consideration to these changed circumstances when considering this application. I am not going to repeat my arguments. The minister knows this is the only all-weather transport available to 100,000 people in the interior of British Columbia. The population is producing hundreds of millions of dollars worth of material from the mines, smelters, forests and agriculture. I do hope that the minister will see my point of view. My spirits have risen since his appointment. I hope he will discuss this matter with the board of transport commissioners so that we will have at least a daily train service with one day coach and a combination cafe and sleeping car to make certain the people of southeastern British Columbia will be able to travel under all weather conditions. Because of weather conditions, air transport is somewhat irregular in the winter months. Because of winter conditions our roads, particularly over the Princeton highway, are blocked on some occasions. I wish therefore, to make another appeal to the minister and I trust this will be my last.
I should like to direct the minister's attention to the excellent administration of the Castlegar airport which is owned by the 28902-5-171
Supply-Transport
municipalities of Nelson, Castlegar and Kin-naird. There has been a great deal of voluntary labour put into this airport. I like to see that. I think it is good and should be encouraged, especially when we have many citizens who are willing to devote their time and money to certain local projects. I know the department has rendered excellent assistance. There have been improvements in recent months and these are appreciated by the airport committee and by the communities that are dependant upon that airport. But I do suggest, because of the uncertain traffic during winter months, further consideration be given to the study of facilities that would make it possible for traffic to land even when the mountains are covered with clouds. At the present time no aircraft attempts to land if the clouds are lower than the surrounding peaks. I understand that problem has not been settled. It is particularly difficult in this district because of the terrain and the narrowness of the valleys. However, I do urge, on behalf of the different communities concerned, further consideration and study to improve this situation.
Now, in addition to that, because of the terrain and nature of our country, we have -I do not know their technical designation because I am a backwoodsman and I find these technical terms difficult to grasp-airports for the landing of aircraft on water, when they are equipped with water skis. We have one at Nakusp and at one or two other places. When these are being proposed I urge the minister to give assistance by way of advice in respect to their location and maintenance. The local groups who build them do so at no cost to the department or the people of Canada, and they are providing a very necessary service. The same applies to one or two smaller ports for planes that land on wheels. The officials of the department should render any assistance they can with respect to the location of these fields and their operation.
I have found in one or two cases that the people concerned were rather ignorant of the regulations and things of that sort. This is not an expensive matter and it is a service that would be much appreciated.
In recent months and years certain companies in the forest industry have been granted booming rights in bays along the Kootenay lake, the Arrow lakes and the Columbia river. This is very necessary for the storing of logs, but I would ask the minister to tell his officials to make certain that the navigable channels on the Columbia river, between Revelstoke, and Arrowhead are kept open for water craft, and to see

Supply-Transport
that no booms are allowed to be strewn across these channels which would prevent craft travelling through them.
Where this has happened it is possibly due to the oversight of some local official who does not understand the law or the regulations, and I urge that the officials be advised to see to it that these booms do not atfect the navigable portions of the channels.
A year or two ago I brought up the necessity of having luminous plates placed on booms and boom anchors. These anchors are usually logs tied to a cement post in the bottom of a lake, or are heavy objects to which the booms are chained. When the booms are taken away a single log is left, and in some cases these single logs have proved to be a great hazard to navigation.
There are several near navigable channels on Kootenay lake, and the companies now operating on that lake place these phosphorescent plates on stationary booms and boom anchors. They can be seen at night by people navigating small craft, and I ask that the same regulations be enforced on the Arrow lakes and the Columbia river. The number of these booms is increasing, and sometimes the single anchor is left a long distance from shore and cannot be seen on a dark night by persons navigating small craft. All that is required is that a plate be attached to either side of the anchor or boom.
Another matter which should receive attention is the acceptance of responsibility for the clearing of snow from wharves, and the sanding of wharves. I am speaking of wharves constructed by the federal government, which I understand come under the administration of the Department of Transport, which usually uses the local public works supervisor, or someone like that, as its agent.
Some of these wharves have a 10 per cent grade and are used by people loading ships and barges. They become very icy and dangerous, and no one has assumed responsibility for clearing the snow from all these wharves. I think the department should make certain that in all cases they are properly cleared of snow and sanded when required for the safety of the public. In some instances the provincial authority does this work because the local foreman sees it as his responsibility; but this is not certain enough.
I also suggest signs should be placed on all wharves to prevent caterpillars, used by logging companies, travelling over them and damaging them with their very sharp cleats. Most of the operators are very good in that respect and lay down planks so that the cats can load onto barges or ships without cutting a wharf to pieces. But it only takes two or three trips with a 35 ton or 40 ton cat to rip
[Mr. Herridge.l
the deck of a wharf to pieces. In this connection more attention should be paid to the enforcement of regulations governing travel of caterpillars over government wharves, because with their large cleats they can do so much unnecessary damage.
I am trying to be as brief as possible, as usual, but there is another matter I wish to bring to the minister's attention, concerning the operation of the Great Northern Railway between the international boundary and Nelson. This railway is owned in the United States and administered in Canada by a superintendent in the United States. I have found on one or two occasions, and in fact reported it to the board of transport commissioners, that the superintendent has ignored the request of ranchers along the railway to undertake to do the fencing required by law. In fact ranchers have lost cattle which were killed on the track because the Great Northern Railway, United States owned and administered, does not provide the fencing that is required by law.
I suggest that the minister's officials keep a close watch on the superintendent who is in charge of this division in Canada. He has admitted some responsibility but is a little inclined to drag his feet. I suggest that the minister give him a bit of a shove from behind.
Another thing I wish to bring to the minister's attention concerns the freight rates charged on this railway. There are people in the area who ship forest products on it, particularly fence poles and posts to the prairies, but the freight rates charged by the Great Northern to transport these forest products from a point near the international boundary to Nelson, where they are transferred to the Kettle Valley Railway, are so high in relation to the rest of the transportation that it makes it almost impossible for these persons to operate at a profit.
I had one letter of complaint in the early part of the session with regard to this matter, and I have had another letter from a second man since then. The board should keep a sharp eye on the administration of this small railway-it is about 30 miles long-to see that Canadian citizens' rights are not overlooked, just because the line is administered by officials in the United States.
There are a large number of launch clubs in the Kootenays. In fact people have taken a greatly increased interest in small water craft since the second world war, and groups have formed clubs to develop this interest as recreation for the people of the communities concerned. In addition there are large numbers of commercial craft, small tugs and things

of that sort, which have replaced the stern-wheelers that operated on the rivers up until 1957.
A great number of people have been concerned about the possibility of accidents with these small craft. In fact we had one unfortunate drowning a year or two ago because a boat was not equipped with the equipment required by law at that time. I urge that the department take a strong stand with respect to regulations governing the equipment that should be carried by these small craft, and governing their operation. I think the police get their best co-operation from the organized groups of launch clubs and organizations of that kind. The need for this type of strict enforcement is growing daily; that is why I bring it to the attention of the minister. I know he is interested, and I know about the conferences; but I want him to know about these things because in the district I have the honour to represent many people are concerned about them.
I have two other points, Mr. Chairman, with respect to aids to navigation. We are getting a great number of water craft coming up the Columbia river from as far south as Portland. As a matter of fact my son-inlaw had 22 United States craft tie up at his residence on the Saturday before last Labour day which had come from as far south as Portland along the Columbia river. I understand that a total of about 175 such craft came up this river last year. These people had just begun to realize where the Garden of Eden is situated and where there are opportunities for 300 miles of magnificent water transportation.
These people require navigation aids. Quite a bit has been done by the department in installing navigation aids between the international boundary and in the narrows between the upper and lower Arrow lakes and between Arrowhead and Revelstoke. I brought this matter to the attention of the former minister and his officials and, as I say, quite a lot has been done. But more could be done, particularly in the narrows between the upper and lower Arrow lakes. The department should make sure that signs are erected which people can understand. It is not good enough to put an oil can up on a tree and paint it red. A man comes along often knowing nothing about this route and he wonders what he should do when the sign says he is supposed to go so many chains, where he should turn and steer to a white cross. I think more of these markers should be erected; a map should be made available for people to purchase and upon it these markers should be indicated. This should also be done in connection with the Kootenay river and Kootenay lakes. People 28902-5-1711
Supply-Transport
should be able to understand what these signs mean. We have had a number of craft run aground between Arrowhead and Revelstoke because people simply did not understand what the signs meant. They got out of the channel and on to sand bars, and so on. I do urge that greater consideration be given to more adequate markers on the river and the issuance of maps showing what these markers mean.
The mines and technical surveys branch have promised for some time to publish a map of this sort. When inquiries have been made as to why this has not been done, the answer has been that they have been too busy on other things. Surely someone in the department could be given the job of marking these markers on the map and writing a code thereon as to what they mean. I do urge, Mr. Chairman, that this matter be brought to the attention of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.
My final recommendation is this. The activities of the Department of Transport cover a very wide field and what they do affects a large number of people. To realize that this is right one has only to look at the row of handsome officials in the gallery this afternoon.

My hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre says order. I am not supposed to mention people whom I am not supposed to see; but I cannot help seeing them. There are a great many people in various departments that are concerned with these matters, who have the responsibility for the regulations covering the operation of small water craft, and so on. People are uninformed in many respects as to what the department is doing and the information that it available. I do suggest that the minister give consideration to having appropriate officials give an occasional talk to suitable organizations in various communities that are particularly concerned with the administration of the Department of Transport in so far as it is related directly to their daily lives. With those few remarks, Mr. Chairman, I conclude this spontaneous address.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks about the ferry service between the mainland of Canada and Newfoundland. At the present time there is one car ferry in service between Port aux Basques and North Sydney. It has been noted that during the summer months this ferry is not able to cope with the demand for service and this need will undoubtedly increase, now that the trans-Canada highway is being proceeded with at a more accentuated

Supply-Transport
pace in the province of Newfoundland. The suggestion has been made within the province that the real need is for additional service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. While I do feel strongly that the present service is inadequate and this will become more apparent, as I have suggested, I do not think that ferry service between Port aux Basques and North Sydney should be confused with the need for an east coast ferry to the province of Newfoundland. This matter has been discussed and I understand that a great deal of work has been put into it. For this we must congratulate the former minister of transport and his department. I am sure the present minister is giving this matter his full attention, but I would like to say a few words about it.
The second ferry to Newfoundland will provide an alternate route and a service to the residents on the east coast of Newfoundland. I am informed that the great majority of the cars which now travel to the island do not proceed all the way to the east coast. Undoubtedly with a paved road across the island this will change somewhat. But I feel the addition of the east coast ferry will mean that a greater number of people will be attracted to travelling all the way across Newfoundland because they will be able to return by a cheaper and shorter route, the east coast ferry.
I am concerned, and I think this concern will grow when the road is completed, as I have suggested, that an east coast ferry in addition to the existing service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques will be inadequate. In fact it is inadequate at the present time. I would therefore make two suggestions for the consideration of the minister. One is that the possibility of purchasing a second hand ferry should be looked into. This ferry need not be of the icebreaker type because it would only be needed, primarily at least, in the summer or fall months to meet the demand which exists at that time of the year. I understand that these ferries can be purchased in a number of places in the world at a very nominal price.
There is some suggestion that this is not a popular move because these things should be built in Canada. If we are already undertaking a sizeable expenditure to provide a second ferry to Newfoundland, it would seem to be in order, to meet the growing need, that a second hand ferry be purchased to go into operation, I would suggest, between North Sydney and Argentia, and at a later date it could go into operation between North Sydney and Port aux Basques. One other suggestion I would like to make is this. It has been suggested to me as a possibility that

we could make use of, I believe they are called C-44's, the aircraft that is capable of carrying 10 to 12 cars. I think it would be a wise course if this suggestion were looked into as a possible means of transportation between Sydney and Stephenville airport on the west coast of Newfoundland. This type of service may reduce the overload on the existing ferry and may in some way be an attempt to meet the growing demand for service between the ports of Port aux Basques and Sydney.
I would say in closing, Mr. Chairman, that the people of Newfoundland are very anxious to have this matter of their ferry service taken care of. They are continually reminded of the fact that between the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia there are five ferries, I believe, in operation and they do not understand why it is they have only one. Therefore, I hope that very shortly we shall have an announcement pertaining to the east coast ferries and that the minister will find time to look into the two matters I have suggested.

Mr. Chairman, on item 1 I am sure the minister is faced, and will be faced, with a great many applications from the railways to abandon certain sections of their lines. This is a complex problem and a very perplexing one which will not be the subject of any quick decisions. However, I have one or two matters I would like the minister to consider. When a railway gets permission to abandon a line, does the right of way revert to the crown? Do the mineral rights on the right of way also revert to the crown? All hon. members are reasonably familiar with the development of rail transportation in western Canada, and the government of the day gave large grants of land to encourage the railways to provide a service to the people and for the future. They gave both the surface rights and the mineral rights. I agree that 60 years ago those mineral rights did not appear to be valuable, but the surface rights were important. I feel that today when a railway receives permission to abandon a section of line providing a service for which they were paid, an adjustment should be made so that the mineral rights, or at least a percentage of them, will revert to the crown.

Mr. Chairman, in taking part in a discussion of the estimates of the Department of Transport I should like to discuss the Trent canal and its possibilities for increased tourist trade. In my constituency the main tourist attraction is the Trent canal system. This deep-water system consists of many locks linked by various rivers and narrows, as well as the locks and channels of the Trent canal. The canal lift lock at Peterborough

which lifts boats to a height of 65 feet, is the highest hydraulic lift lock in the world, and I was very glad to see that the minister has in his estimates $175,000 for the work on this lift lock. I should like to ask the minister to attempt to have the work started as soon as possible after the close of the season so as not to interrupt travel on the Trent next spring.
The Trent canal attracts the largest number of pleasure craft in Canada. In 1959 the lockage of the Trent canal was 61,935, the highest in the nation. This figure was more than three times the 20,510 recorded in 1954. The canal system was built over 50 years ago and is a compliment to the engineering of that era. The money which the Conservative government set aside to beautify and restore this system during the last parliament should not be pared in any way, because this system brings to Canada millions of tourist dollars each year. It has been said that 24 tourists daily equal a $100,000 industry. This should be very interesting to the new Minister of Industry. More than 450 resorts and camps cater to visitors in the Kawartha lakes area, and the permanent summer population of tourists and visitors is more than 100,000 people. Our summer visitors in the Peterborough area total many more than one million each year. This is why we feel we should not pare estimates for our canal systems. Canada has in the Trent a tremendous tourist attraction which is only now approaching its potential as a tourist dollar earner.
Now that I have spoken of the potential of the Trent as a tourist dollar earner I should like to point out the inadequacies of the methods employed on the Trent system. I refer particularly to the opening and closing of the locks. I do not think it is fair to these employees to subject them to the drudgery of opening locks in the same manner as they were opened over 40 years ago. There has been a start made to electrify them, but this should be speeded up. I understand the hon. member for Northumberland is opening a new lock at Fenelon Falls tomorrow.
I should like to be there.

Perhaps we should all be there. I feel the system has been neglected too long, both from the standpoint of the people operating the locks and from the standpoint of the people operating the boats.
I also want to make reference to the low level bridges which are found on the Trent system. There are several of them in my constituency. Surely it is about time in this day and age that we eliminate these places where boats have to stop in order that bridges may be turned. These are things which hurt our tourist industry. Both boats and highway
Supply-Transport
traffic are held up while bridges are being turned. I know of two such places in my riding on busy highways, and I understand the Ontario department of highways has plans to correct this if they get support from the Department of Transport. Such things are very annoying to our tourists. I feel that we should get rid of these obstacles so that we can invite tourists from the United States, who are used to electrification of locks, to enjoy our canals. The prospect is that many more boatmen from the United States will use this water highway.
I should like to refer to the recommendations in volume 3 of the Glassco report, where they recommend a toll system to assist in the cost of operating our canals. I am afraid this will cost the Department of Transport more in supervision than they could realize from the rentals. An alternative to this problem, which I feel would help to give some revenue to these systems and to the tourist industry, is the tax that the Ontario government refunds on gasoline used for marine purposes. If this amount of money were put back into the upkeep of these canals for our tourists there would not be a need for tolls or wharf rentals. In Ontario for the year ending March 31, 1962, the government refunded to the boating public the sum of $610,000, and it was estimated that another $600,000 was not claimed. This amounts to $1,210,000. This money is realized from an 11 cents per gallon refund on gas used in motor boats. At the present time I have not the figures of refunds received by people in the province of Quebec or the other provinces across Canada. To bring these tax refunds into the federal system, it would mean an adjustment between the provincial and federal governments. We realize that the boating industry is growing every year. Lockage on the Trent system is increasing by 10 per cent every year. Along with this increase in the use of the Trent, the operation and maintenance costs of the system have increased. In addition to this there are costs of rebuilding and replacing the locks. This has been estimated over a ten-year period to be over $12 million.
In conclusion, may I say there are a few other areas of this waterway in which I should like to see some improvement. There should be sewage disposal tanks provided in appropriate areas so sewage could be pumped from boats. No sewage should be emptied from cruisers or houseboats into our canal systems.
Our locks should be open from early morning until sundown to service the public properly. Men working on the locks should not be asked to work seven days a week from eight in the morning until late at night. If there were a double shift, it would be a help

Supply-Transport
to the men operating the locks and give better service to the tourists. In closing, I should like to say that we should get on with the completion of this waterway in order to help balance our tourist trade with the United States.

I am anxious to make a few comments with reference to transportation because questions of transportation are, indeed, the essence of the economic problems in the maritime provinces and, in particular, in my constituency of Halifax.
The present freight rates policy of this nation coats the martime arteries of transportation, interfering with the economic and healthy flow of goods through those arteries. As you know, Mr. Chairman, the Atlantic development board has already indicated it will investigate the effect of the St. Lawrence seaway both in the past and in the future upon the maritime economy. I hope the Minister of Transport will pay close attention to the results of this investigation because, if we in the maritimes are to be helped, the greatest thing that the Atlantic development board or the area development agency of the new Department of Industry or, indeed, any other branch of the government could do would be to use the transportation facilities which exist in this nation, and particularly the government-owned railway, so as to provide something closer to a postal stamp system of freight rates so that manufacturers in all parts of the country would have an equal opportunity to ship their goods elsewhere. This would be the best way of making the maritime region self-supporting and prosperous, along with the rest of Canada. If this were done we would find there would not be these large areas which lag so badly behind the rest of the nation in economic development, as do the Atlantic provinces and some other areas.
In the constituency of Halifax our largest industry, and the backbone of our economy, is the port of Halifax and the handling of the goods which historically go through our waterfront, both in the course of importation to Canada for use in the central Canadian market and in the course of export by the manufacturers of Ontario, Quebec, and the central region. The handling of these goods both coming and going provides employment on the waterfront of Halifax. Traditionally, Halifax, along with Saint John, New Brunswick, has been the major winter port of this country. But there is no rail or freight subsidy on goods imported or exported through maritime ports. These goods are carried at the normal freight rates of the railway. We have been placed in an increasingly disadvantageous position and have suffered economic hardship because of the
[Mr. Stenson.l
growing extent of subsidies to other means of transportation, particularly since the completion of the seaway. Throughout the length of the St. Lawrence we see a subsidy on navigation aids. Aids must be given to navigation from the time a ship enters the St. Lawrence river proper to the time it reaches Montreal and, of course, beyond that, on the seaway itself.
Another subsidy to transportation on the St. Lawrence river is in the form of dredging, which is done at federal expense. Another is the use of icebreakers, which has increasingly lengthened the St. Lawrence shipping season to the disadvantage of the maritimes. Another subsidy to transport on the St. Lawrence river is pilotage in the river proper, as distinct from pilotage in the harbours which are on the way. This type of expenditure is not needed outside harbours in the Atlantic region because pilotage is not necessary on the open sea. In addition, on the seaway itself we have artificially low tolls which do not return the amounts of money which have been invested in this great and forward looking water system.
As a result of all these circumstances, the port of Halifax is this summer suffering from loss of business. We have had in the Halifax area the quietest summer along the waterfront in many years. Each year has become a little worse. Even within the past month or two, shipping lines which carry goods to Africa have found there are competitors who are willing to go to the head of the seaway. I do hope that while he is waiting for the results of this over-all investigation by the Atlantic development board the minister will consider immediate measures to stop any further erosion of business from our port at the present time. Of course, every ship which changes its ports of call and abandons the port of Saint John or the port of Halifax makes the situation more acute because frequency of sailing is about the most important thing a port can offer when it goes looking for goods to be shipped. If a port cannot offer frequent sailings it cannot interest manufacturers, exporters or importers in using its facilities. Thus, when we lose certain ships or established lines there is a chain reaction which hurts us in other ways.
We heard the Minister of Trade and Commerce announce in this house two or three days ago that the government intended to spend $40 million in new or extra aid to underdeveloped countries by providing them with food, presumably flour and wheat. I would urge the government to consider channelling a large proportion of these additional exports through the maritime ports. In this way we would receive some measure of

immediate help. I know that recently there have been instances of shipments of grain and flour specifically destined for Poland having gone through the port of Vancouver, even though Vancouver was so busy that ships were waiting to be loaded. I hope that the Minister of Transport will continue to keep a close watch on this situation and do everything possible for the assistance of transportation in the maritime provinces because only when we have a comprehensive freight rates system, indeed something close to a postal stamp type of freight rates system, will it be possible for the maritimes to be prosperous again. In this regard I also want to say that the continued use of the port of New York both for the export of Canadian goods and the import of goods into Canada should be curtailed in some manner by the government for the greater economic benefit of Canadian ports.
To turn to one other subject very briefly, Mr. Chairman, there is in the Department of Transport estimates the usual deficit, although not a large one, for the ferry operating between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor which transports passengers, passenger cars and trucks. The service provided by the motor vessel Bluenose is of very great importance to the tourist industry in Nova Scotia, but I feel that at the present time it is inadequate and there is great need for a second ferry, particularly for the summer months, on the run from Bar Harbor to Yarmouth. The Bluenose has been successful on this run, where earlier attempts at a ferry service between New England and Nova Scotia resulted in astronomical losses. The present service operates between the closest two points, thus enabling the Bluenose to make a return run the same day. In the days of the service from Boston this was not possible, and I submit that if a second ferry is added at any time it should also operate with Bar Harbor as the United States terminal.
The recent announcement of a new national park in western Nova Scotia adds importance to the service of the motor vessel Bluenose because it will be a further impetus for tourists from the United States to come to that part of the province. In connection with the present operation of the service I should like to say that from my own very recent experience I do not feel that tourists and other passengers intending to travel on the boat receive the attention and courteous service at the Bar Harbor terminal in Maine that is necessary, if they are to have a good initial impression of Canada when they arrive in Nova Scotia. While this terminal may be operated by the American authorities, I do not think the average traveller fully realizes this, and it is very much to the advantage of this
Supply-Transport
country in helping to develop the tourist industry that we impress upon those connected with the terminal at Bar Harbor that people travelling to Nova Scotia should be treated with the utmost courtesy.
There are also some other flaws at that terminal. I am informed by people who made the trip during the past week that the motor vessel Bluenose sailed on two or three occasions at least from Bar Harbor, with less than her capacity of cars, even though there were tourists waiting in the area to travel on the boat who then had to wait until the next day. This inefficiency should certainly be remedied.
My final words, Mr. Chairman, are with reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway ferry service between Digby and Saint John. As hon. members know, the Princess Helene was recently retired from service and replaced by the former Princess of Nanaimo, now renamed the Princess of Acadia.
A good ship.

That may be. While I am sure that the Princess of Acadia has a very large capacity for passengers, those who live in the area say that she does not carry enough trucks. Again, this is a problem of transportation for western Nova Scotia in that we should be able to ship our fish and all our goods as easily as possible. If the Princess of Acadia cannot carry an adequate number of trucks, then she is not providing the necessary service. Indeed, the necessary service to afford efficient transportation will never be provided until we have a car ferry operating between Digby and Saint John. Only then will Nova Scotia have ferry service provided by the two railways rather than ferry service provided by one railway plus a service in the form of a loose liaison between the Dominion Atlantic Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway through the use of the Princess of Acadia.

Mr. Chairman, I just want to say a word or two on a project which I am sure will be close to the heart of the minister, inasmuch as he is an Ottawa valley member and has always taken quite a personal interest in it. I am speaking of the Ottawa river seaway from Montreal to Georgian bay. I do not want to embarrass the minister at this time about canals because I know he already has a canal in Quebec, the Soulanges, which he is trying to get rid of, but with no bidders. However, I want to bring this project to his attention. He is familiar with many of the details and I am also quite sure he is aware that a year or two ago his department undertook a survey to determine the economic

Supply-Transport
possibilities of the Ottawa seaway. I know that the survey was undertaken but I do not know what stage the survey has reached. Perhaps the minister would like to inquire about this and report to me or to the committee any findings which his officials have made.
In that connection he may also recall that the Department of Public Works undertook a feasibility survey of the Ottawa river seaway from the engineering point of view. This survey was based exclusively on engineering data already in the possession of the department and consisting primarily of a report made in 1908 following a very extensive survey instituted by the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, which took four years. This was followed by another survey in 1927.
As a result of the survey made last year I believe the engineers of the Department of Public Works were in agreement that from an engineering point of view there was no insurmountable obstable to the canal being built. This more or less placed the onus upon the Department of Transport, which is interested in the economic aspects of the project.
There are various steps, of course, by which this project may be achieved. One of the first steps would be to make the city of Ottawa accessible to sea navigation by making the city of Ottawa or some port in the neighbourhood on the Quebec side into a seaport accessible to ocean going traffic. I think this is a practical project. Although no official report has been issued as far as I know, the information I was able to obtain from the Department of Public Works indicated that it would cost about $100 million to achieve this first stage of the over-all project which would open the whole of the Ottawa river and lake Nipissing and the French river to ocean navigation, right through to Georgian bay.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the minister in his investigation of the matter to determine the economic benefits to be derived from the projects might also take a look at another proposal which, in my view, is closely linked to the Ottawa river seaway. I refer to a proposal known as the Grand canal which is being promoted in a very vigorous manner by an engineer from Sudbury, Mr. James Kierans. This project, if implemented, would provide a means of paying for part of the cost of the canal. The plan would be to divert waters that are now flowing uselessly into James bay into the Ottawa river system and eventually having that flow of water reach the great lakes to replenish the low level of water that exists in the great lakes now. This need has reached crisis proportions, especially for cities such as Chicago on the south side of the great lakes.
[Mr. Martineau.l
As the minister knows, there has been extensive lobbying in the United States to permit the lowering of levels in the great lakes. So far, the pressure in that direction has been resisted. At one stage I believe the then president of the United States, Mr. Eisenhower, vetoed a project which would have enabled the cities in the United States along the great lakes to take a greater supply of water, thereby lowering the general level of the great lakes. The current project envisages the flow of great masses of water down the French river and into the great lakes, and also it envisages the possible sale of water. Water is a raw material, and it is a much needed raw material that is becoming in shorter supply as the years go by and as the need for it increases.
This project I believe will bear investigation by the officials of the department, especially in the light of the possibility of opening the Ottawa river to deep sea navigation. This project, of course, has been mooted with varying degrees of intensity throughout the years since confederation. I believe the time is fast approaching in this country when we should make greater utilization of the very important natural resources which we have for water transportation. Water transportation is more and more being exploited in the United States, and particularly in Europe. Certainly if there existed in Europe any waterway with potentialities for navigation, such as the Ottawa system, it would have been utilized long ago. I know the conditions are not the same. I know the minister will say it is going to be a costly project. This is true, but it is a project that must be visualized not only for tomorrow or the next ten years, but perhaps for the next 50 or 60 years.
One result of the construction of this project, as the minister is aware, would be the opening of great sectors of northern Ontario and northern Quebec to intensive industrial development. If a seaway of the proportions of the St. Lawrence seaway is not possible at this time, then at least some start should be made on opening the Ottawa to barge traffic. There is quite an amount of bulk traffic that could be carried by that means. I hope, therefore, the minister will ask his officials to intensify and accelerate the economic survey in order to determine what steps in the project could be implemented now, what possibilities there are for water traffic, what possibilities there are for the development of new hydroelectric power from the project and also what possibilities there are of making a deal with the United States for the purchase of new fresh water supplies.

I believe this summarizes my thoughts on the subject. I know the minister has a personal interest in this matter, and I feel he will be doing something along these lines.
