speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the next time the minister has an opportunity to answer points that have been raised, I hope he will make a statement on two matters about which I should like to remind him. First, I wish he would bring us up to date on the T.C.A. maintenance and overhaul base at Winnipeg. As the minister knows, all of us from Winnipeg, indeed all of us from Manitoba, who were present when the Manitoba delegation appeared before the government on June 18, were delighted with the statement made by the Prime Minister. We were led to have hope that the employment provided at the T.C.A. base in Winnipeg would be retained there. There have been indications, even since then, that something is being done about this matter. Perhaps the minister could bring us up to date. Perhaps he could tell us how the firm of R. Dixon Speas and Associates is getting along with the inquiry it is making. Perhaps he could tell us what the situation is with regard to this matter, which is of great importance to the employees who are affected and, we feel, of importance to the aviation picture in Canada.
The other matter about which I should like to hear from the minister is related to the pension situation of Canadian National employees who are already retired. As the minister knows, this is a subject which has often been raised in this house over the past years. On April 13, 1962, the then prime minister announced in the house changes that had been made in the pension plan of Canadian National Railways, improving the pension position of those who were still employees. Although the announcement was made on April 13, the effective date of those changes was April 1, 1962. At that time the former prime minister was asked what was being done for those who were retired prior to April 1 of that year. Of course, the answer was that that was another matter that had to be looked into upon another occasion.
I make two points in connection with the announcement made by the former prime minister on that occasion. The first is that it is always contended, and I agree, quite properly, that this is a matter that is in the hands of the management of Canadian National Railways. I also have in mind the role of pension committee. Nevertheless, when the former prime minister made his announcement in 1962, he indicated a decision had been arrived at as a result of discussions between the Canadian National Railways and the government. Since the government came 28902-5-172
Supply-Transport
into the picture on that occasion, it seems to me that it might well come into the picture with regard to the matter of improving the pensions of those already retired.
The other point I wish to make arising out of what was said on April 13, 1962, is that an improvement was then made with respect to service that had been given many years before. We are frequently told when we raise questions about the pension position of people who are about to retire, or are already retired, that there is a contractual element in all of this and that we must not hope to have it changed. But certainly on that occasion the contractual element, so far as early years of service was concerned, was changed, and I think that is something that is not unreasonable for us to request for employees previously pensioned.
As a matter of fact in 1959 this was done with respect to retired employees of the federal civil service. We have often been told when we plead for an improvement in the position of retired government employees that this would interfere with the contractual arrangement, but at least the former government did find a way in 1959 to improve the position of civil servants already retired. This was done through the Public Service Pension Adjustment Act of 1959.
Because something was done to improve the position of Canadian National employees still to retire, with respect to their earlier service, and because something was done by the federal government to improve the position of civil servants already retired, I think it is not unreasonable for us to continue asking for an improvement in the pension position of Canadian National Railways employees already retired.
As the minister knows, because it was his parliamentary secretary who placed the facts on record in Hansard, there is quite a bit of information on the present situation to be found in Hansard of June 3, 1963, at pages 542 and 543. That information was given in answer to perennial questions of mine regarding the amounts of pension being drawn by retired C.N.R. employees.
If I may summarize the figures from the pages I have just noted, there would seem be a total of 23,833 persons drawing Canadian National Railways pensions. These vary from very small amounts to larger sums, in fact sums of $200 a month and over; but I emphasize the fact that of this grand total there are 377 persons who are drawing pensions of less than $25 a month. There are also 2,559 whose pensions are just $25 a month.
There is a footnote on pages 542 and 543 which explains why some of these people are drawing such small pensions, but even the foonote does not explain away the fact that

Supply-Transport
pensions of these amounts are very low. If one looks further at these tables and does a little simple arithmetic, he discovers that out of the 23,833 pensioners 7,148, or 30 per cent of them, are drawing pensions of less than $50 a month. I offer one further statistic. Out of that same total of 23,833 some 12,357, or 56 per cent, are drawing pensions of less than $100 a month from the Canadian National.
I submit that in this day when we are moving into an acceptance of the view-and I am very happy to see it-that the pensions of people who have worked should be pensions that provide adequate retirement, these amounts being drawn by people who are already retired should not be left that way. In passing may I say that I hope the discussions that are taking place today not far from this building will not interfere with certain plans to provide adequate retirement pensions.
However, I must insist that it is not good enough just to improve the pension plans of those still working. It is not good enough to just say that people who will retire 10 or 15 years from now will do pretty well. This is no consolation to those already retired who through their efforts have brought the Canadian National Railways, our economy and our country to the position that now obtains.
I urge the minister not to give the stock answer, that this is something to be left to the Canadian National Railways. The former government met the management and came up with an improved pension plan. It also did something for retired civil servants, and I shall have something more to say about retired civil servants when we come to the item covering them.
At this time we are talking to the head of the Department of Transport and I urge that he bring up in cabinet the whole question of what might be done to augment the pensions of these retired C.N.R. employees, and particularly of those in the lower and middle brackets.
I am interested in many aspects of the work in the minister's department, but on this occasion I thought I would just ask for a statement on these two important subjects, the question of retaining the T.C.A. maintenance and overhaul base at Winnipeg, and improving the pensions of C.N.R. employees already retired.

With respect to the closing of railway lines, some have been closed in my constituency and at present there are two stations in process of being closed. The closing down of one of these will cause great inconvenience to the local citizens, who will have to travel some 15 miles to the nearest station. I am referring specifically to the

station at Douglas, which is actually located in North Renfrew but is very close to the borders of my constituency. If this station is closed the citizens will have to travel some 15 miles to Eganville, and this will be a great inconvenience.
I appreciate that railroads have to be put in a more economic condition than they are in at present, but I suggest it is not purely and solely a question of balance sheet economics. Those of us who have appeared before the board of transport commissioners when the closing of stations or lines was contemplated, have seen that the yardstick is apparently the balance sheet, how many dollars can we save, the question of present use, public convenience and necessity, but there are other considerations which must be taken into account at the policy making level, the cabinet level. These questions concern the future growth and future need of areas for railway service.
One thing that appears to be happening, which is not in the best interests of the country at large, is that this closing of stations and lines, as I understand it, is apparently only one aspect of the recommendations made by the MacPherson commission, and I suggest that those recommendations, if they are to be implemented, should either be implemented in toto or generally revised.
In that connection I would point out that in this session of parliament there has been demonstrated on this side of the house the fact that we are committed to short range and long range planning, and that we intend to see to it that the country develops along some planned scheme and not helter-skelter, as has been the case in the past. This being so, I suggest the question of railways should be treated in the same way.
We should not implement one small facet of the MacPherson report, namely the closing of stations or lines for economic reasons, unless we have a broad, new, comprehensive and planned railway policy which will include the social ramifications of the closing of these lines and stations. In other words, I do not think it can be purely a matter of dollars and cents and the immediate return or reward to the railways, as we are now considering it. In particular in the west end of my riding I have a situation, Mr. Chairman. This part of the country, the area around Barrys Bay, Killaloe and Brudenell used to be a very profitable and prosperous lumbering area. There was a day when this created employment and prosperity for that area, and now to a very large degree the forest resources have been depleted for many years and no secondary industry has come in by virtue of distance from markets, and the fact that there is no trained labour pool. Industry is not going to come into these areas

unless some encouragement is provided. I think such plans as the economic council, the Department of Industry and the new tax concessions may provide that type of incentive. But at the same time I do not think we should forget the transport aspect in this regard; that in these areas even roads are inadequate.
Surely we cannot hope to have secondary industries coming into these areas in the future unless there is adequate transportation for them both by road and by rail, and adequate service by way of stations situated in localities which will best serve the communities. Even though today it might be more economic for the railways to close these stations, I think we should look at the long term and the planning aspect and see whether, if we intend these areas to survive and develop economically in the future, we should not preserve the railways where they are needed for that future growth. 1 would remind the committee, Mr. Chairman, that at the time these charters were granted to the railways they were given monopolies and they made very large profits in some of these areas, particularly in areas such as the west end of my riding. When the lumbering industry was at its peak the railways were very happy to have those monopolies and to make these very large profits in those areas.
Such being the case, I do not think we should look only at last year's balance sheet. We should see whether those railways have made profits in past years, and if so, surely it is not asking too much to have them put back something from those profits they made in past years into these areas for future development and to encourage their future growth and industrialization. In these areas even some slight factor might make the difference between obtaining or not obtaining industry. Goodness only knows, there is little enough incentive for secondary industry to come into areas such as the west end of my riding. Hydro rates are higher than those in the metropolitan areas. If we take away this last resource of rail transportation and rail service we are in effect abandoning these areas in so far as future economic growth is concerned.
Mr. Chairman, I would like to say one word in respect of the Ottawa river, which is also in my constituency. It bounds my constituency and that of my hon. friend from Pontiac-Temiscamingue. There we have a community of interest.
And Carleton.

The river does bound Carleton, but Carleton is my neighbour to the east. I was very interested to hear the remarks of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue 28902-5-172a
Supp ly-Transport
in this regard and 1 certainly associate myself with those remarks. I will be glad to provide any humble support that I can in respect of the request he made. Even before we reach the, I think very lofty and proper goal that he has as an end, I would suggest it would be in order, and should be done in the immediate future, in this area for the Department of Transport to embark upon a plan for building more wharves and loading devices along that river. There was a day when the Ottawa river was purely and simply a vehicle for the lumbering people to carry their logs to market. I think if one were to total up economically the value of the Ottawa river today, it would be found to be far more valuable as a tourist asset, as a summer resort asset than it is even to the lumbering industry. I suggest this has been accomplished with but little help from any arm of government; that by virtue of its natural attributes the area has developed as a tourist resort. But I think at this time help is needed to develop it even further. I remind the committee that this is an area of low employment. If we are to develop this area even further as a tourist resort, I suggest that the Department of Transport would contribute something very valuable in doing the following things. These can be done more immediately, possibly, than the long term plan which has been mentioned.
We could immediately build more wharves and loading platforms in this area. I think this would be extremely important to the growth of tourism. We should have a method whereby boats can be immediately transported over the dams and rapids. I think there are methods by which this can be done economically. I am instructed that it could be done very economically with the installation of a narrow gauge rail, so that boats could be transported across the hydro dams and so that tourists might travel, without the necessity of great expenditures in pleasure craft all the way from the St. Lawrence river to lake Temiscamingue. This could be done without the expenditure of a great deal of money. The first thing would be more wharves and more loading platforms for boats. The second thing would be a method of transporting boats across the present hydro dams so that a vast area which is today of only limited access to tourists and the boating public could be opened up, and a new era of tourism could loom in the future for the Ottawa valley. I think this could be done, as I have said, without spending a great deal of money and at the same time it would be a very facile and ready way of creating immediate employment which is now so badly needed in the area.

Supply-Transport
In the west end of my riding the areas of Combermere and Barrys Bay are a potential and undeveloped tourist paradise. A great deal could be done by the Department of Transport in building more wharves, more loading devices for boats, more locks so that one could travel from one lake to another. I think this would attract a great deal more United States tourist money in that area, which we need so very badly in order, among other things, to help us with our international balance of payments. This could be done without embarking upon any great program of expenditure. There is already on the books a plan for the building of a dam at Galeairy lake, Whitney. In spite of my efforts to that end to date, these plans have not been brought to fruition. I think these things should be hurried. If we are to be progressive, if we are to provide employment, this is the kind of thing we should do, and at the same time we would be developing a very important industry and a new area which has not to date been sufficiently opened to tourism.
One other aspect of the matter I should like to bring to the attention of the minister is this. I again go back to the question of the Ottawa river and the fact that its chief economic use is now as a tourist resort. Over the years the logs have come down this river in order to reach their ultimate destination, and many of these logs have sunk to the bottom of the river and today are sticking up all over the place, embedded in the bottom, some for hundreds of years. They create a very serious menace to the boating public. There have been serious accidents and it may be that some day there will be a fatal accident if these things are not looked after.
Here, I suggest, is where the Department of Transport could play a very valuable and useful part in opening up this area to more attractive tourism. It would create a new and interesting attraction to the tourist industry in this particular area where the great opening of the Ottawa river is, at Chats lake with Norway Bay on the Quebec side and Sand Point, Braeside and Arnprior on the Ontario side. If the river at this point could be cleaned up and the deadheads taken up from the bottom, this would improve the situation. The Department of Transport is in charge of navigable streams, and although this is not an easy job it would create employment for many people for a considerable period of time. It would also remove a hazard in the river and achieve the economic objective of creating a new and attractive tourist resort. I think this would be in the interests of the country as a whole, and the people of that area in particular.

Mr. Chairman, at this stage of the debate on the estimates of the Department of Transport, I should like to draw the minister's attention on two matters which are of particular interest to my constituency: air lines and the Canadian National Railways.
As far as air lines are concerned, we do not seem to mean much today, because even if for the past few years we have had a magnificent landing strip located, to be more exact, on the limits of the town of Roberval, we have not yet succeeded in obtaining a regular service.
The minister will recognize that if the previous government had found it advisable to provide the necessary grants for the construction of that landing strip, it is because its need had been established for a long time. Then why is it practically deserted today, since it only accommodates the flow of tourists who, each year, invade the lake St. John area to head for our lakes and streams which, for fishing, are known as the best to be found in the province of Quebec.
This airport is an important asset for our tourist trade but in order to make our tourist service complete, we must think necessarily of an airport located within Dolbeau itself, because at the present time, in our opinion, the Roberval airport is quite inadequate by itself to meet the demand of the U.S. visitors who pour into our district. That is why we are asking the minister to investigate the situation.
I made a survey of my own in order to find out why the regular air transport companies did not use the Roberval airport and I beg of the minister to lend me his valuable assistance in order to settle this problem because it is unthinkable that such a deficiency should be allowed to continue. To begin with, I do not understand why the present service between Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec city up to Seven Islands through Bagotville should not also include on its route, the Roberval airport.
In fact, the people of Roberval and vicinity are always reluctant to go to an airport located four counties away in order to catch a plane when it would be so easy to authorize the scheduled flight to make a stop-over in Roberval. I ask you a question, Mr. Minister, and the people of Lake St. John are anxious to receive an answer. We are not begging, we are merely asking a very logical thing. I hope that you will not forget to take this

request into consideration when allotting your estimates.
I know that some people will object that such a service would be uneconomic, without even trying to support their allegation. Moreover, certain administrators can only give one answer: not profitable. It is much simpler than to make some effort to provide an adequate service in every area. The minister is convinced, I am sure, that an efficient service is essential to transportation. Every effort should be made to achieve that aim.
Mr. Chairman, as far as the C.N.R. is concerned, I inquired last year about having repairs made to our railway tracks and the only answer I got was an acknowledgment. Public bodies have also taken some steps in that connection, and I have here the last letter from the chamber of commerce of my county, of which I sent a copy to the department.
It was said, among other things:
We, of the Roberval chamber of commerce, propose, as part of our next year's activity, firmly to approach the board of transport commissioners finally to settle the renovation of our national railways line, Quebec via Dolbeau and Chicoutimi. We are already working on a well-informed brief which we will, in due time, transmit to you in order to support and defend that most important cause in our district. Among permanent projects, we do not believe that there are any more important projects than that one to give work to our unemployed on a permanent basis, at least for a few years to come.
I received such letters, sir, from nearly every town and city asking me to exert some pressure on the C.N.R. in order to have our lines improved.
Today, I see that your government is broadminded enough to understand our needs. You may be assured, sir, that the whole district will be happy to know of your effort to further the use of railways as means of transportation.
It may be said today that the railways are having fewer customers. But there is a reason for it. It is probably due-and I do not know whether you have already wondered about it-to the fact that the real object of a railway company has been forgotten, which is to give adequate service. It is all very well to build skyscrapers, to pour the taxpayers' money into terminal buildings in the larger centres, which buildings are getting the more vast and splendid as our local stations disappear. But I think that some
Supply-Transport
mistake was made in this respect, in that the money has been all invested in those grand buildings while the main thing was forgotten, that is to improve the tracks.
I am of the opinion that if stations had been built for the railroad and not the railroad for the stations, the C.N.R. would not have to regret a loss of patronage.
If you want to be convinced of my allegations, you need only to come to my riding, not in the luxurious car of the president of the C.N.R., but in the ramshackle car used by private members of parliament. I am convinced that when you arrive at Dolbeau, you will say, like 50 per cent of railway patrons: I will not be caught at it again. I wish to draw the minister's attention to this: they should put more emphasis on service, as service means improvement of the railway.
Even if railway officials have plush offices in skyscrapers, if they force patrons to travel in 30-year old cars, they will always have to face the same problem.
I have mentioned to you those two important points, sir, and I am sure that you will take my remarks into consideration.

I have one brief question I should like to direct to the minister. I wonder if when he replies to the various questions which have been directed to him during the afternoon he would answer this one. Can he give us any fresh information or encouraging word as to progress in the construction of that great project, the Vancouver international airport?

I have a few brief remarks to make on a subject which, according to the papers at least, is very close to the minister's heart, namely the work of the research and rescue organization on the great lakes. My own interest in the subject has existed for a good many years. In 1954, I brought this question before the house in a motion and later on, in 1956, the minister of transport of that day, Mr. Marler, took a considerable interest in the matter and was responsible for drawing up a number of regulations concerning the use of small boats. Later still, the minister of transport who succeeded him took a similar interest in the subject and extended the search and rescue organization on the great lakes. I believe one or two ships are under construction and that one of them is already in service.
Such measures are obviously necessary because in the last ten years the number of small boats on the great lakes has, I suppose, quadrupled. I know that as many as 1,600

Supply-Transport
small boats go out on lake Erie from one little port, Turkey Point, when the bass fishing opens. Every week we read the accident toll on the water during the week end, and the loss of life through drowning and accidents involving small boats has begun to reach a scale we associate with the highways. I know the minister is interested in this subject. I have read in the papers reports of what he is doing and I hope he continues on this course. Many newspapers have carried editorials on this subject lately, requesting more action. We all know that everything cannot be done at once but as long as we can continue to make steady progress in this field it will be to the advantage of all the people of this country. Only yesterday I read an editorial on the subject in the London Free Press. Articles on the subject frequently appear in the Toronto Globe and Mail as well as in other papers. There are many organizations which help look after research and rescue work on the great lakes. Apart from the Department of Transport ships there are the Ontario provincial police, the R.C.M.P., volunteers from R.C.A.F. squadrons and so on. Various municipalities also have facilities for helping to rescue people who meet with accidents on the water.
For the sake of hon. members who are not familiar with the great lakes, let me say that these large bodies of fresh water can become exceedingly rough in a very short period of time. I do not wish to spend much more time discussing the situation because I have spoken about it repeatedly over the years and I know the minister has these things at heart. But there is a suggestion I should like to make to him. I have already mentioned that there are facilities to assist search and rescue work carried out by Department of Transport boats, R.C.A.F. teams, local authorities and the like. One of the problems seems to be that if anyone gets into trouble no one knows who to get in touch with. What is needed is a coordinator who has had some brief training so that he or she would know immediately whom to contact. Since most of these problems arise during the summer months I agree it would not be practicable for the department to take on a large extra staff of co-ordinators. What could be done might be to use senior university students. They could receive a brief course before taking up their work and act as co-ordinators, on the lakes, on other large inland waters and perhaps even on the seacoast as well. These would be third or fourth year students, and they would be engaged in the summer months to co-ordinate all the assorted search and rescue facilities I have mentioned. If anything happened, if someone got lost, or a boat overturned, it would be reported to the 
co-ordinator who in turn would immediately contact the proper facilities. Many drowning deaths arise because it takes too long to rescue the victims. What is really needed is a co-ordinator and I think such a person could be most helpful.

May I take just a few minutes in which to express the hope that the minister will give consideration to a matter which I believe requires his immediate attention. Though I do not know the exact figures, I presume millions of dollars are spent on air search and rescue. I know we all agree that a magnificent job has been done by those who take part in air search and rescue, and it will continue to be done. But is it not high time more effort was made, by law or by regulation, to place responsibility upon those who operate private planes and who are responsible for the majority of the air search and rescue work which takes place? It is my understanding that in British Columbia this year there have been seven crashes and that they involved a number of deaths. Yet in looking over the situation I am surprised to find that in a great many cases American private planes that come into Canada do not have to file a flight plan and do not have to advise anyone exactly how long they are going to be in Canada. So we have the situation of a private plane crossing our border, not filing a flight plan and not advising anyone as to where it is going or how long it is going to be in our country. The result is that in the event of an accident we are faced with a great expenditure.
I have also had it brought to my attention that far too many of those who pilot private planes in Canada do not file flight plans. In addition, although we have certain regulations with regard to safety equipment on private planes many of these planes do not have this equipment on board and there is practically no checking of private planes to see that they have the required equipment.
In view of the extensive cost to the government and therefore to the taxpayers of Canada of air search and rescue, surely we are not unjust in insisting on proper equipment in private planes, proper inspection of private planes and that when a plane leaves the ground somebody should be told where the pilot thinks he is going and when he anticipates arriving there.
I do not want to hold up the committee, but I feel that such a piece of equipment as the SARAH would be most useful. From all I have read it would appear that this very cheap electronic equipment is crashproof, and in the event of a crash it automatically sends out signals that can be picked up by those who are conducting the search. I

simply want to bring this matter to the attention of the committee because air crashes and fatalities are reaching substantial proportions and the higher they go the greater the cost to the government and the taxpayers. If these people will not do these things voluntarily, surely we have a right to ask that there should be regulations and laws to bring about conformity to common decency in the operation of planes in Canada.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Will the house leader, in view of the heat wave, give us a very short statement of the business for Monday only?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will endeavour to be brief. According to an order issued last night by the house, on Monday we will take the various stages of the resolutions and bills respecting the remuneration and pensions of members of parliament. Then, if there is the consent of the house, we will take the same stages in the judges' measure. In any event, we will certainly take the resolution stage. I would not want to ask for third reading of either of those two bills because I believe they should stand over until the following day. We would like, if we could, to finish the excise tax in committee, and if the house were agreeable to have third reading.
Then there is a bill on which I believe there would be almost no debate. It is required under law that if a bridge is to be built over the St. Lawrence river there must be a statutory provision for it. The bill has passed the other house and has been before us for some time. I believe the work is being held up because we have not acted, and I would hope there might be a possibility of facilitating it without too much delay.
After that, if there should be any further time, we would start the committee stage on the economic council. I would prefer not to say anything about any day after Monday because the Prime Minister promised to report to us.
It being thirteen minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
